Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\,\,y=\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,0<t<\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t=x \\ y=\operatorname{tan}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t=y\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Pythagorean identity ${\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t=1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t & =1 \\ {\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t & =1-{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t \\ \operatorname{sin}t & =\sqrt{1-{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We used here that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t>0$ in the range $0<t<\frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, using the definition of a tangent, we obtain

$$
\operatorname{tan}t=\frac{\operatorname{sin}t}{\operatorname{cos}t}=\frac{\sqrt{1-{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t}}{\operatorname{cos}t}.
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡t=x$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡t=y$ into this formula, we get

$$
y=\frac{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}{x}.
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=\frac{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}{x}.$

question.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}2t,\hspace{1em}y={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t,\hspace{2em}0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{12}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{12},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{12}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=2{t}^{2}+3,\,y=3{t}^{5}+{t}^{3},\,0\le t<\infty ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}(5{t}^{2}+1).
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{3{t}^{2}(5{t}^{2}+1)}{4t}=\frac{3t(5{t}^{2}+1)}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{3(1)(5(1)^{2}+1)}{4} \\  & =\frac{18}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=\frac{4}{\pi }{t}^{2},\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{8}{\pi }t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{(\frac{8}{\pi }t)}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{2t\operatorname{sec}⁡t}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{sec}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)}{\pi } \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \sqrt{2})}{\pi } \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨2x,3,2⟩$, $\mathbf{b}=⟨x,1,-1⟩$ and $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|=\sqrt{93}.$ Find $x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2x & 3 & 2 \\ x & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}2x & 2 \\ x & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}2x & 3 \\ x & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(-3-2)\mathbf{i}-(-2x-2x)\mathbf{j}+(2x-3x)\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-5,-4x,x⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{(-5)^{2}+(-4x)^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+16{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{17{x}^{2}+25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we solve for $x$ the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{93} \\ \sqrt{17{x}^{2}+25} & =\sqrt{93} \\ 17{x}^{2}+25 & =93 \\ 17{x}^{2} & =68 \\ {x}^{2} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\pm 2.$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨-3,2,0⟩,$ $\mathbf{b}=⟨2,-4,2x⟩$ and $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|=\sqrt{77}.$ Find $x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 2x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -4 & 2x\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ 2 & 2x\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(4x-0)\mathbf{i}-(-6x-0)\mathbf{j}+(12-4)\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨4x,6x,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{(4x)^{2}+(6x)^{2}+(8)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+36{x}^{2}+64} \\  & =\sqrt{52{x}^{2}+64}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we solve for $x$ the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{77} \\ \sqrt{52{x}^{2}+64} & =\sqrt{77} \\ 52{x}^{2}+64 & =77 \\ 52{x}^{2} & =13 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\pm \frac{1}{2}.$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨-1,2x,3⟩,$ $\mathbf{b}=⟨2,-x,1⟩$ and $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|=\sqrt{355}.$ Find $x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -1 & 2x & 3 \\ 2 & -x & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2x & 3 \\ -x & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2x \\ 2 & -x\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(2x+3x)\mathbf{i}-(-1-6)\mathbf{j}+(x-4x)\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨5x,7,-3x⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{(5x)^{2}+(7)^{2}+(-3x)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{x}^{2}+49+9{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{34{x}^{2}+49}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we solve for $x$ the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{355} \\ \sqrt{34{x}^{2}+49} & =\sqrt{355} \\ 34{x}^{2}+49 & =355 \\ 34{x}^{2} & =306 \\ {x}^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\pm 3.$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨4,x,3⟩,$ $\mathbf{b}=⟨-2,3,0⟩$ and $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|=\sqrt{181}.$ Find $x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 4 & x & 3 \\ -2 & 3 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}x & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}4 & 3 \\ -2 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}4 & x \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(0-9)\mathbf{i}-(0+6)\mathbf{j}+(12+2x)\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-9,-6,12+2x⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{(-9)^{2}+(-6)^{2}+(12+2x)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{81+36+144+48x+4{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{261+48x+4{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we solve for $x$ the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{181} \\ \sqrt{261+48x+4{x}^{2}} & =\sqrt{181} \\ 261+48x+4{x}^{2} & =181 \\ 4{x}^{2}+48x+80 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+12x+20 & =0 \\ (x+10)(x+2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-10,\,-2.$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨0,3,4⟩,$ $\mathbf{b}=⟨-1,-x,2⟩$ and $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|=\sqrt{221}.$ Find $x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 0 & 3 & 4 \\ -1 & -x & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 4 \\ -x & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -1 & -x\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(6+4x)\mathbf{i}-(0+4)\mathbf{j}+(0+3)\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨6+4x,-4,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{(6+4x)^{2}+(-4)^{2}+(3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36+48x+16{x}^{2}+16+9} \\  & =\sqrt{61+48x+16{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we solve for $x$ the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{221} \\ \sqrt{61+48x+16{x}^{2}} & =\sqrt{221} \\ 61+48x+16{x}^{2} & =221 \\ 16{x}^{2}+48x-160 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+3x-10 & =0 \\ (x+5)(x-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-5,\,2.$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨0,-2,3⟩,$ $\mathbf{b}=⟨-2,1,-2x⟩$ and $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|=\sqrt{53}.$ Find $x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 0 & -2 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 & -2x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 3 \\ 1 & -2x\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -2 & -2x\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(4x-3)\mathbf{i}-(0+6)\mathbf{j}+(0-4)\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨4x-3,-6,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{(4x-3)^{2}+(-6)^{2}+(-4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{x}^{2}-24x+9+36+16} \\  & =\sqrt{16{x}^{2}-24x+61}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we solve for $x$ the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{53} \\ \sqrt{16{x}^{2}-24x+61} & =\sqrt{53} \\ 16{x}^{2}-24x+61 & =53 \\ 16{x}^{2}-24x+8 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-3x+1 & =0 \\ (2x-1)(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2},\hspace{0.167em}1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\frac{1}{2},\,1.$

question.:question/problem: For which of the following vector fields is $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y$ a potential function?
question.:question/worked-solution:
A vector field $\mathbf{F}$ is conservative if it is the gradient of a scalar function $f.$ That is, there exists a function $f$ such that $\mathbf{F}=\mathrm{∇}f.$ The function $f$ is called a potential function for $\mathbf{F}.$

To compute the vector field associated with a potential function $f,$ we compute its gradient.

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{F}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field that has $f$ as a potential function is

$$
\mathbf{F}=2x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}.
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=(ay-2x{y}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ where $a$ is a constant. Given that $\mathbf{F}$ is conservative, find the value of $a.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=P(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ be a vector field with domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$\mathbf{F}$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

For the vector field $\mathbf{F},$ we have $P=ay-2x{y}^{3}$ and $Q=x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=a-6x{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1-6x{y}^{2}.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a-6x{y}^{2} & =1-6x{y}^{2} \\ a & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a=1.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=\frac{axy}{{x}^{2}+1}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ where $a$ is a constant. Given that $\mathbf{F}$ is conservative, find the value of $a.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=P(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ be a vector field with domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$\mathbf{F}$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

For the vector field $\mathbf{F},$ we have $P=\frac{axy}{{x}^{2}+1}$ and $Q=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{ax}{{x}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{ax}{{x}^{2}+1} & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ ax & =2x \\ a & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a=2.$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following vector fields are conservative on ${R}^{2}?$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

Note that for each of our functions, $D={R}^{2}.$ With this in mind, let's check each of the vector fields. 

- For the vector field $F,$ we have $P=2x-y$ and $Q=-x.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-1.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $F$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $G,$ we have $P=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)$ and $Q=x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy),\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy).
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $G$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $H,$ we have $P={e}^{x-y}$ and $Q=-{e}^{x-y}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{e}^{x-y},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-{e}^{x-y}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $H$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $F=(2x-y)\,i-x\,j$; $G=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,i+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,j$; $H={e}^{x-y}\,i-{e}^{x-y}\,j$.

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following vector fields are conservative in their respective domains?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

Note that for each of our functions, $D={R}^{2}.$ With this in mind, let's check each of the vector fields.

- For the vector field $F,$ we have $P=2x-4y$ and $Q=4x-8y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are not equal, we conclude that $F$ is not conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $G,$ we have $P={2}^{2x+y+1}$ and $Q={2}^{2x+y}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}={2}^{2x+y+1}\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={2}^{2x+y+1}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $G$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $H,$ we have $P=2x\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1)$ and $Q=\frac{2{x}^{2}y}{{y}^{2}+1}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{4xy}{{y}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{4xy}{{y}^{2}+1}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $H$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $G={2}^{2x+y+1}\,i+{2}^{2x+y}\,j$; $H=2x\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1)\,i+\frac{2{x}^{2}y}{{y}^{2}+1}\,j$ only.

question.:question/problem:
![](images/0b/0bc0e75bb577ca37b89568e14a4e0d03da7ce4f4853c4e8c57d9b2df79897b13.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- Statements “$F$ is irrotational” is true. Since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ the vector field $F$ is irrotational.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{curl}\,F=0$; “$F$ is irrotational” only.

question.:question/problem: Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=3{z}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k},$ what is $\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+R\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the curl of $\mathbf{F}$ is the vector field given by

$$
curl\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=\mathrm{∇}\times \mathbf{F}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 3{z}^{2} & 2y & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(2y)]\mathbf{i}-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(3{z}^{2})]\mathbf{j}+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{z}^{2})]\mathbf{k} \\  & =(0-0)\mathbf{i}-(0-6z)\mathbf{j}+(0-0)\mathbf{k} \\  & =6z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}={e}^{y+z}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+xyz\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$ Evaluate $\mathrm{∇}\times \mathbf{F}$ at the point  $(2,1,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+R\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the curl of $\mathbf{F}$ is the vector field given by

$$
curl\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=\mathrm{∇}\times \mathbf{F}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ {e}^{y+z} & 1 & xyz\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(1)]\mathbf{i}-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)-\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{y+z})]\mathbf{j}+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y+z})]\mathbf{k} \\  & =(xz-0)\mathbf{i}-(yz-{e}^{y+z})\mathbf{j}+(0-{e}^{y+z})\mathbf{k} \\  & =xz\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+({e}^{y+z}-yz)\mathbf{j}-{e}^{y+z}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(2,1,-1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F})(2,1,-1) & =2(-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+({e}^{1+(-1)}-1(-1))\mathbf{j}-{e}^{1+(-1)}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =-2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1,\,y=\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ \frac{2}{3}(x+1) & =\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ \frac{4}{9}{(x+1)}^{2} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2 & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ \frac{2}{3}(y+2) & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  \\ \frac{4}{9}{(y+2)}^{2} & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9}{(x+1)}^{2}+\frac{4}{9}{(y+2)}^{2} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  \\ 4{(x+1)}^{2}+4{(y+2)}^{2} & =9 \\ {(x+1)}^{2}+{(y+2)}^{2} & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation of the circle is ${(x+1)}^{2}+{(y+2)}^{2}=\frac{9}{4}.$

question.:question/problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2},\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2},\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-\frac{1}{2}) & =5\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ \frac{1}{5}(x-\frac{1}{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ \frac{1}{25}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+\frac{1}{2}) & =5\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ \frac{1}{5}(y+\frac{1}{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ \frac{1}{25}{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{25}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{25}{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  \\ \frac{1}{25}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{1}{25}{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =1 \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $$
\displaystyle {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(y+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}=25.
$$

$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & ={(\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{25}{4}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & ={(\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{25}{4}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}

Adding the two equations and using ${\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta =1,$ we get

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{25}{4}.$

question.:question/problem: Given that $y=\sqrt{3-6x},$ find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=3-6x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-6.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-6) \\  & =-\frac{3}{\sqrt{3-6x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $g(x)=3x+4$ and $f(g(x))=g(x{)}^{5}.$ 

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(g(x)) & =({g}^{5}{)}^{′}=5{g}^{4}, \\ {g}^{′}(x) & =(3x+4{)}^{′}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={f}^{′}(g(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x) \\  & =5{g}^{4}\cdot 3 \\  & =15(3x+4{)}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{1-4x}$ at the point where $x=-2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=1-4x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-4) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-4x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-2} & ={\left(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-4x}}\right)|}_{x=-2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-4(-2)}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression ${\operatorname{cos}}^{3}\theta {\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{cos}}^{5}\theta .$

question.:question/problem:

\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}x{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+\operatorname{sin}x{\operatorname{cos}}^{4}x}{\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{sin}x}=
$$

First, we factor the numerator:

$$
\frac{{sin}^{3}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{4}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\,
$$

Next, we use the Pythagorean identity to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, and then we simplify the resulting expression as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x\cdot 1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that

$$
\frac{{sin}^{3}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x{cos}^{4}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Hence, we conclude that

question.:question/problem:

$$

First, we factor $\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ from the first two terms of the numerator:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{cos}x{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}x+\operatorname{sin}x{\operatorname{cos}}^{3}x+1}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{sin}x({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x)+1}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x}
$$

Next, we use the Pythagorean identity to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, and then we simplify the resulting expression as much as possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{sin}x({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x)+1}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{sin}x\cdot 1+1}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{sin}x+1}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{sin}x}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x}+\frac{1}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{sin}x\cdot \operatorname{sin}x}+\frac{1}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}x\enclose{updiagonalstrike}{\operatorname{sin}x}}{\enclose{updiagonalstrike}{\operatorname{sin}x}\cdot \operatorname{sin}x}+\frac{1}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}x}{\operatorname{sin}x}+{\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}x}\right)}^{2} \\  & =\operatorname{cot}x+{\operatorname{csc}}^{2}x\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{cos}x{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}x+\operatorname{sin}x{\operatorname{cos}}^{3}x+1}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x}=\operatorname{cot}x+{\operatorname{csc}}^{2}x.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Simplify the trigonometric expression $$
\displaystyle \operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the first term using the definition of $\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$ This gives

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$

Now, we put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x}-\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}x}{\operatorname{sin}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{sin}x}-\frac{(1-\operatorname{cos}x)\operatorname{cos}x}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x} \\  & =\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}x-{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x} \\  & =\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x-(\operatorname{cos}x-{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x)}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x} \\  & =\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x-\operatorname{cos}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify using the Pythagorean identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x-\operatorname{cos}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x} & =\frac{({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x)-\operatorname{cos}x}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x} \\  & =\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}x}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that:

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}=\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\displaystyle \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta }+\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta }+\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta } \\  & =\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta }+\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta } \\  & =\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify using the Pythagorean identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta } & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta } \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{csc}\theta \operatorname{sec}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .
$$

question.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression $\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{1+\operatorname{sin}x}+\operatorname{sin}x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{1+\operatorname{sin}x}+\operatorname{sin}x & =\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{1+\operatorname{sin}x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{1} \\  & =\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{1+\operatorname{sin}x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}x(1+\operatorname{sin}x)}{1(1+\operatorname{sin}x)} \\  & =\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+\operatorname{sin}x(1+\operatorname{sin}x)}{1+\operatorname{sin}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify using the Pythagorean identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+\operatorname{sin}x(1+\operatorname{sin}x)}{1+\operatorname{sin}x} & =\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+\operatorname{sin}x+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x}{1+\operatorname{sin}x} \\  & =\frac{({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x)+\operatorname{sin}x}{1+\operatorname{sin}x} \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{sin}x}{1+\operatorname{sin}x} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{2+\operatorname{sin}x}+\operatorname{sin}x=1.
$$

question.:question/problem: $1+\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}1+\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta } & =\frac{1}{1}+\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{1+{sin}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )}{1\cdot (1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )}+\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{1+{sin}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }+\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta } \\  & =\frac{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify using the Pythagorean identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta } & =\frac{1+1}{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta } \\  & =\frac{2}{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
1+\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }=\frac{2}{1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }.
$$

question.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression $\operatorname{sin}x-\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{sin}x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}x-\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{sin}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{1}-\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{sin}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}x(1-\operatorname{sin}x)}{1-\operatorname{sin}x}-\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{sin}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}x(1-\operatorname{sin}x)-{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{sin}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify using the Pythagorean identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}x(1-\operatorname{sin}x)-{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{sin}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}x-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x-{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{sin}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}x-({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x)}{1-\operatorname{sin}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}x-1}{1-\operatorname{sin}x} \\  & =\frac{-(1-\operatorname{sin}x)}{1-\operatorname{sin}x} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\operatorname{sin}x-\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{sin}x}=-1.
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$

$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The function $\mathbf{F}$ can be expressed in terms of its components $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ as

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=P(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},
$$

where

$$
P(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-y),\,Q(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

We first find the domain of each component function. Then, we compute their intersection to find the domain of $\mathbf{F}:$

- The function $P(x,y)$ is defined when the expression under the logarithm is positive. So, to find the domain, we solve the following inequality:

$$
x-y>0\,⟹\,x>y.
$$

Therefore, the domain of $P$ is given by

$$
{D}_{1}=\{(x,y)\in {\mathbb{R}}^{2}\hspace{0.222em}|\hspace{0.222em}x>y\}.
$$

- The function $Q(x,y)$ is defined everywhere other than when the denominator vanishes. To find where the denominator vanishes, we set it equal to zero and solve:

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=0\,⟹\,x=y=0
$$

Therefore, the domain of $Q$ is given by

$$
{D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\in {\mathbb{R}}^{2}\hspace{0.222em}|\hspace{0.222em}(x,y)\ne (0,0)\}.
$$

Finally, the domain $D$ of $\mathbf{F}$ is given by

$$
D={D}_{1}\cap {D}_{2}=\{(x,y)\in {\mathbb{R}}^{2}\hspace{0.222em}|\hspace{0.222em}x>y\}\hspace{0.167em}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={e}^{3t}+1,\,y={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=0$ on the curve. Determine the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=0$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={e}^{3\cdot 0}+1=1+1=2, \\ y & ={e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)=0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=3{e}^{3t},\,{y}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)),
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))}{3{e}^{3t}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)}{3{e}^{2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=0,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=0} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)}{3{e}^{2\cdot 0}} \\  & =\frac{0+\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,0)$ and the slope $m=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =\frac{\pi }{3}(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =\frac{\pi }{3}(0-2) \\ y & =-\frac{2\pi }{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(0,-\frac{2\pi }{3})$ is the $y$-intercept.

The tangent line is vertical if ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${y}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$

Note that ${y}^{′}(0)=9\ne 0.$ Therefore, we conclude that when $t=0,$ the tangent to the curve is vertical.

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}),\,y=2{t}^{3}-3t\,,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=1$ on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{2})=\operatorname{ln}⁡1=0, \\ y & =2(1)^{3}-3(1)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $(0,-1).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{2}{t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=6{t}^{2}-3
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{6{t}^{2}-3}{\frac{2}{t}} \\  & =\frac{6{t}^{3}-3t}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$  the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =\frac{6(1)^{3}-3(1)}{2}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\,}=-\frac{2}{3}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,-1)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=-\frac{2}{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+1 & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot (x-0) \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=7(t-1),\,y=2{t}^{3}-18t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Determine the points at which the normal to the curve is vertical.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The normal is vertical if the tangent is horizontal. Therefore, we require ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=7,\,{y}^{′}(t)=6{t}^{2}-18.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
6({t}^{2}-3)=0\,⟹\,t=\pm \sqrt{3}.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(-\sqrt{3}) & =7\ne 0, \\ {x}^{′}(\sqrt{3}) & =7\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed vertical when $t=\pm \sqrt{3}.$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed horizontal when $t=\frac{1}{2}.$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$ 
Evaluate $\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F}$ at the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf{F}$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F}=\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}y) \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}y-{e}^{x}(-\operatorname{sin}y). \\  & =2{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}$ at the point  $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F})(0,\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2{e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) \\  & =2\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=(x-y)^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(y+z)^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(x+z)^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$ Evaluate $\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(-2,2,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+R\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf{F}$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F}=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-y)^{3})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((y+z)^{3})+\frac{∂}{∂z}((x+z)^{3}) \\  & =3(x-y)^{2}+3(y+z)^{2}+3(x+z)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(-2,2,2),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}(-2,2,2) & =3((-2)-(2))^{2}+3((2)+(2))^{2}+3((-2)+(2))^{2} \\  & =3(-4)^{2}+3(4)^{2}+3(0)^{2} \\  & =96.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/b3/b315be9ba524ab538388fdaad31161c280d7d6e5ab71261345063ac6ffe819d5.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement $∇\cdot F>0$ is true, whereas statements $∇\cdot F=0$ and $∇\cdot F<0$ are false. Notice that the lengths of the vectors increase as we move vertically and horizontally away from the origin. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a source at every point.

- Statement “$F$ is solenoidal” is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is $∇\cdot F>0$ only.

question.:question/problem:

$$

$$

what are the ranges of $x$ and $y?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ notice that for $0\le \theta <2\pi ,$ we have $-1\le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ -1+3 & \le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +3\le 1+3 \\ 2 & \le x\le 4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $2\le x\le 4.$

- To find the range of $y,$ notice that for $0\le \theta <2\pi ,$ we have $-1\le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ -1-1 & \le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1\le 1-1 \\ -2 & \le y\le 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $-2\le y\le 0.$

Therefore, the ranges are $2\le x\le 4$ and $-2\le y\le 0.$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following vector fields are conservative on ${R}^{2}?$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

Note that for each of our functions, $D={R}^{2}.$ With this in mind, let's check each of the vector fields. 

- For the vector field $F,$ we have $P=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and $Q=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are not equal, we conclude that $F$ is not conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $G,$ we have $P=3{e}^{3x+2y}$ and $Q=2{e}^{3x+2y}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=6{e}^{3x+2y},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=6{e}^{3x+2y}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $G$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $H,$ we have $P=2xy$ and $Q={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $H$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $G=3{e}^{3x+2y}\,i+2{e}^{3x+2y}\,j$; $H=2xy\,i+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j$ only.

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=({y}^{3}-ay)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(3x{y}^{2}-2x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$, where $a$ is a constant. Given that $\mathbf{F}$ is conservative, find the value of $a.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=P(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ be a vector field with domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$\mathbf{F}$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

For the vector field $\mathbf{F},$ the domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ and we have 

$$
P={y}^{3}-ay,\,Q=3x{y}^{2}-2x.
$$

 

Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3{y}^{2}-a,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{y}^{2}-2.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}-a & =3{y}^{2}-2 \\ -a & =-2 \\ a & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a=2.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=({y}^{2}+2xy)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+({x}^{2}+2axy)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$, where $a$ is a constant. Given that $\mathbf{F}$ is conservative, find the value of $a.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=P(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ be a vector field with domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$\mathbf{F}$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

For the vector field $\mathbf{F},$ the domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ and we have 

$$
P={y}^{2}+2xy,\,Q={x}^{2}+2axy.
$$

 

Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y+2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x+2ay.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2y+2x & =2x+2ay \\ 2y & =2ay \\ 2y-2ay & =0 \\ 2y(1-a) & =0 \\ 1-a & =0 \\ a & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a=1.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=(ax{y}^{2}+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(4{x}^{2}y+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$, where $a$ is a constant. Given that $\mathbf{F}$ is conservative, find the value of $a.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=P(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ be a vector field with domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$\mathbf{F}$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

For the vector field $\mathbf{F},$ the domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ and we have 

$$
P=ax{y}^{2}+1,\,Q=4{x}^{2}y+1.
$$

 

Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2axy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=8xy.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2axy & =8xy \\ 2axy-8xy & =0 \\ 2(a-4)xy & =0 \\ a-4 & =0 \\ a & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the last equality must be satisfied everywhere on $D,$ we conclude that $a-4=0,$ that is, $a=4.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}(x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x{y}^{2}+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $\mathbf{F}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+1)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)) \\  & ={y}^{2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(0,\pi /2)} & ={\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}^{2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}-0 \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}xy\,dx+(x+1)\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
question.:question/worked-solution:
Green's theorem states that 

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/e6/e69bc348e36b05955d1eaa9eda4516afe137056ead176a46a4fc11bb887ed166.png)

Since $P(x,y)=xy$ and $Q(x,y)=x+1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}xy\,dx+(x+1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta )\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le r\le 3,\hspace{0.222em}0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}r-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}2({r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}2{r}^{3}({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}2{r}^{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\frac{81}{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{2}[\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{81}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{81\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/bc/bcdc0f59fa284c2b1f1621e7de057ef6f0e084d2eca6732fbc5eae3f74ede113.png)

Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{C}(\sqrt{5+x}-3{x}^{2}y)dx+({e}^{-{y}^{2}}+3x{y}^{2})\,dy,
$$ where the path $C$ is shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/62/6273034b38059d3d49b2a29c91052c290151b4a29073f1c925172dd1c4c2bf72.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)=\sqrt{5+x}-3{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={e}^{-{y}^{2}}+3x{y}^{2},
$$

we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-3{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{5+x}-3{x}^{2}y)dx+({e}^{-{y}^{2}}+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{y}^{2}-(-3{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,2\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}3({r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{4}3{r}^{3}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{4}{r}^{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{2}^{4}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}60\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =180[\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =180\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =90\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to evaluate $$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r},
$$ where $$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=⟨\frac{\sqrt{x+5}-{y}^{3}}{3},\frac{\sqrt{y+5}+{x}^{3}}{3}⟩
$$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ oriented counterclockwise.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}={∮}_{C}\frac{\sqrt{x+5}-{y}^{3}}{3}\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}x+\frac{\sqrt{y+5}+{x}^{3}}{3}\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}y.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/09/09a69771617d73af6e4a1a42720223951e2e6edeb71a8df4d12aeb1bc22031aa.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{x+5}-{y}^{3}}{3},\,Q(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{y+5}+{x}^{3}}{3},
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\frac{\sqrt{x+5}-{y}^{3}}{3}\,dx+\frac{\sqrt{y+5}+{x}^{3}}{3}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-(-{y}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta )\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le r\le 2,\hspace{0.222em}0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}({r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =4(2\pi -0) \\  & =8\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=xy\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{x}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =xy=4\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=4{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}t)-(4{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}t{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+8\operatorname{sin}t{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{sin}t{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}-16{u}^{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=3x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=64.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=4\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x=12\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =3y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(12\operatorname{cos}t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}t)-(6\operatorname{sin}t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+24{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =24t\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =24(2\pi -0) \\  & =48\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=(x-16y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=16.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $1,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=4\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},\hspace{2em}0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x-16y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =x+y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{cos}t-16\operatorname{sin}t)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}t)-(4\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-16\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t+16\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t+4{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =4t\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =4(2\pi -0) \\  & =8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)={x}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=7\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=4x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=8\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+6\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
question.:question/worked-solution:

$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4x=4(8\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=32\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =4y=4(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=24\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-8\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(32\operatorname{cos}t)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}t)-(24\operatorname{sin}t)\cdot (-8\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }192({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }192\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =192t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =192(2\pi -0) \\  & =384\pi \end{aligned}

$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=(1-x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x-y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $16{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=144.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1-x=1-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =x-y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf{T}(t).$

In this case, $\mathbf{n}$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf{T},$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/59/59e503e0c4d950f030891bbaeb7ed890426ef470a1e1dae89d27eabb8dd591a6.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2},\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4y=4t, \\ Q(x,y) & =2x-1=2{t}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4t)\cdot (1)-(2{t}^{2}-1)\cdot (2t)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4t-4{t}^{3}+2t\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6t-4{t}^{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-{t}^{4}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(3-1)-(0-0){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
According to the flux form of Green's theorem, the flux of the vector field 
$\mathbf{F}(x,y)=⟨y+2{x}^{2}y,\hspace{0.222em}{x}^{2}-x{y}^{2}⟩$
across the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(0,0),(2,0),(2,1),$ and  $(0,1)$ can be represented as

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $\mathbf{n}$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C,$ and $D$ is the region bounded by $C.$ Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/98/98d7da0c7cd1e1f1006c1db74ae1a1e1f198d9066df6585745ee36548f0b8d96.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y+2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4xy+(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=2xy.$

question.:question/problem:

$$

through the boundary of the square $-1\le x\le 1,-1\le y\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/35/35e378bca35f4b0822c713556065415d59b5c566ec8fcc8e3124256aac7b7f14.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡y+2x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{5}-3y.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\hspace{0.167em}-1\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-3)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-1)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}x\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{-1}^{1}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(1-(-1))\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & =-2{\int }_{-1}^{1}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & =-2y\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/34/3497b3bbc834879026235f97468f5feb26e91a2b73a4de3da87597bf422ecd33.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)-y{x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+2xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2xy+2x)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2x-2xy)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{2}-{x}^{2}y)\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{1}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[(1-y)-0]\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(1-y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & =[y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-((-1)-\frac{(-1)^{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=⟨xy-\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1},\hspace{0.222em}{x}^{3}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/00/006d80a7dbe4d03b78cc5fb1a642405e3fdfdd69ec9d80014ee8e0355ad1ae73.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=xy-\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{3}+y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \frac{y}{2},\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+1)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y/2}^{y/2}(y+1)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(y+1)[x]_{-y/2}^{y/2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(y+1)[\frac{y}{2}-\left(-\frac{y}{2}\right)]\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{4}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
