through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=y,$ $\,x=-\sqrt{y},$ and the line $y=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/24/24369439bc62cf06084a43d97dff0cee4e4089fd103511ef73d9dd5af1256ebb.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=30xy$ and $Q(x,y)=15{y}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=30y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =30y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):\sqrt{y}\le x\le y,\hspace{0.167em}0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(30y+30y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{y}}^{y}60y\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}y[x]_{-\sqrt{y}}^{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}y(y+\sqrt{y})\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}+{y}^{3/2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y \\  & =60{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+\frac{2{y}^{5/2}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =60(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{2}{5})-0 \\  & =44.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve $\mathbf{f}(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}t,\hspace{0.167em}3\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.167em}4\operatorname{sin}t⟩$ from $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{4}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}t),\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}t),\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.167em}3\operatorname{cos}t,\hspace{0.167em}4\operatorname{cos}t⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+9{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+16{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t)+9{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t} \\  & =\sqrt{9{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+16}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4}‖{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+16}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve $\mathbf{f}(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.167em}{e}^{t},\hspace{0.167em}\operatorname{sin}t-\operatorname{cos}t⟩$ from $t=-1$ to $t=1?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}t),\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t-\operatorname{cos}t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}t-\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.167em}{e}^{t},\hspace{0.167em}\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}t⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}t-\operatorname{sin}t)}^{2}+({e}^{t})^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-2\operatorname{cos}t\operatorname{sin}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{e}^{2t}+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+2\operatorname{cos}t\operatorname{sin}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}‖{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/16/162c0d0310cbbb533c30af373820751fc6c5a447127958486571224d7f8ac07a.png)

Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}t,\hspace{0.167em}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}t⟩$ from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}t),\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}t-\operatorname{sin}t),\hspace{0.167em}{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}t)⟩ \\  & ={e}^{t}⟨\operatorname{cos}t-\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.167em}\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}t⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =|{e}^{t}|\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}t-\operatorname{sin}t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}t)}^{2}} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-2\operatorname{cos}t\operatorname{sin}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+2\operatorname{cos}t\operatorname{sin}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t} \\  & ={e}^{t}\sqrt{2({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t)} \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

For a $2\times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}v & 2v \\ 2 & v+8\end{vmatrix} \\  & =v\cdot (v+8)-2v\cdot 2 \\  & ={v}^{2}+4v\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
and $det(B)=1$, what is the value of $p?$

For a $2\times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =\begin{vmatrix}5-p & p \\ 3 & p\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(5-p)\cdot p-p\cdot 3 \\  & =-{p}^{2}+2p\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨0,9,3⟩,$ $\mathbf{b}=⟨3,2,0⟩$ and $\mathbf{c}=⟨-1,1,1⟩.$ Find $\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the scalar triple product $\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 9 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}-9\cdot \begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix}+3\cdot \begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-9(3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot 0)+3(3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot 2) \\  & =0-27+15 \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{p}=⟨7,4,9⟩,$ $\mathbf{q}=⟨1,2,-2⟩$ and $\mathbf{r}=⟨3,0,5⟩.$ Find $\mathbf{q}\cdot (\mathbf{r}\times \mathbf{p}).$

question.:question/problem: Find $\mathbf{c}\cdot (\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}),$ if $\mathbf{a}\cdot ((-3\mathbf{b})\times (-7\mathbf{c}))=7.$

First, we factor out the constants and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot ((-3\mathbf{b})\times (-7\mathbf{c})) & =7 \\ (-3)\cdot (-7)\cdot [\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})] & =7 \\ \mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{c}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{a}) & =-\frac{1}{3},\end{aligned}
$$

and again we swap $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{c}\cdot (\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}) & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\mathbf{b}\cdot (\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{c}),$ if $\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}=⟨2,5,1⟩$ and $\mathbf{a}=⟨6,1,-9⟩.$

First, we compute the triple scalar product 

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =⟨3,5,-4⟩\cdot ⟨6,-1,3⟩ \\  & =3\cdot 6+5\cdot (-1)+(-4)\cdot 3 \\  & =18-5-12 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{c}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{a}) &=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Determine the equation of the level curve that passes through the point $P(1,1)$ for the function $f(x,y)=xy-2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1) & =1(1)-2 \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the level curve that passes through $P(1,1)$ is the $-1$-level curve.

Recall that the level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ xy-2 & =-1 \\ xy & =1 \\ y & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level curve that passes through $P(1,1)$ is the hyperbola $y=\frac{1}{x}.$

question.:question/problem: Determine the equation of the level curve that passes through the point $P(2,0)$ for the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{x-{y}^{2}+3}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,0) & =\frac{1}{2-{0}^{2}+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2-0+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the level curve that passes through $P(2,0)$ is the $\frac{1}{5}$-level curve.

Recall that the level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=\frac{1}{5}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ \frac{1}{x-{y}^{2}+3} & =\frac{1}{5} \\ 5 & =x-{y}^{2}+3 \\ x & ={y}^{2}+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level curve that passes through $P(2,0)$ is the parabola $x={y}^{2}+2.$

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: $c=0$ gives a parabola, excluding the origin

question.:question/problem:
The level curves of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x+{y}^{2}}{x}$ are given by $f(x,y)=c.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+{y}^{2}}{x} & =c \\ x+{y}^{2} & =cx \\ x(1-c)+{y}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=-1,$ the level curve is $x=-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2},$ which is a parabola that opens to the left (excluding the origin). So, “$c=-1$ gives a line” is false.

- If $c=0,$ the level curves is $x=-{y}^{2},$ which is a parabola that opens to the left (excluding the origin). So, “$c=0$ gives a parabola, excluding the origin” is true.

- If $c=1,$ the level curve is $y=0,$ which is the $x$-axis (excluding the origin). So, “$c=1$ gives the $x$-axis, excluding the origin” is true.

So, the correct answer is “$c=0$ gives a parabola, excluding the origin”; “$c=1$ gives the $x$-axis, excluding the origin” only.

question.:question/problem:
The level curves of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ are given by $f(x,y)=c.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =c \\ {y}^{2} & =c({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) \\ c{x}^{2}+(c-1){y}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=0,$ the level curve is the line $y=0,$ which is the $x$-axis. So, “$c=0$ gives a parabola” is false.

- If $c=1,$ the level curve is the line $x=0,$ which is the $y$-axis. So, “$c=1$ gives an ellipse” is false.

- If $c=2,$  then we obtain 

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=2\,⟹\,2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=0.
$$

However, the only real solution to this equation is  $(x,y)=(0,0),$ which is not in the domain of $f(x,y)$ because it would result in division by zero. Thus, “$c=2$ gives a hyperbola” is false.

So, the correct answer is "None of the listed".

:question/answer-fields.:answer-field/key: $c=1$ gives the line $y=x,$ excluding the origin

question.:question/problem:
The level curves of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x}$ are given by $f(x,y)=c.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x} & =c \\ y & =cx\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=-1,$ the level curve is the line $y=-x,$ excluding the origin. So, “$c=-1$ gives a hyperbola” is false.

- If $c=0,$ the level curve is the line $y=0,$ which is the $x$-axis (excluding the origin). So, “$c=0$ gives the $y$-axis, excluding the origin” is false.

- If $c=1,$ the level curve is the line $y=x,$ excluding the origin. So, “$c=1$ gives the line $y=x,$ excluding the origin” is true.

So, the correct answer is “$c=1$ gives the line $y=x,$ excluding the origin” only.

question.:question/problem: Which of the following represents the level curves of $f(x,y)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡x?$

Notice that the equations $x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡\frac{c}{3}+2\pi n$ do not depend on $y.$ So, for a given $c\in [-3,3]$ and integer $n$, the right-hand side of the equation is constant. As a result, we obtain a family of vertical lines, as shown below.

question.:question/problem:
Given that $$
\mathbf{F}=\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},
$$ what is $\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf{F}$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F}=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\right)+\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\right) \\  & =-\frac{2xy}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}^{2}}-\frac{2xy}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{4xy}{{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $\mathbf{F}=\operatorname{ln}(xy)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+xy\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ what is $\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf{F}$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F}=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}(xy))+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy) \\  & =\frac{1}{x}+x \\  & =\frac{1+{x}^{2}}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=2xy{z}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x{e}^{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+y{z}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$ 
Find $\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+R\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf{F}$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F}=\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy{z}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(y{z}^{3}) \\  & =2y{z}^{2}+x{e}^{y}+3y{z}^{2} \\  & =5y{z}^{2}+x{e}^{y}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=xz\operatorname{cos}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y{x}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+x{z}^{2}{e}^{y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$ 
Evaluate $\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1,0,-2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+R\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf{F}$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F}=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xz\operatorname{cos}y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{x}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{z}^{2}{e}^{y}) \\  & =z\operatorname{cos}y+{x}^{2}+2xz{e}^{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1,0,-2),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F})(1,0,-2) & =(-2)\cdot \operatorname{cos}0+{1}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot (-2)\cdot {e}^{0} \\  & =-2+1-4 \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=x(y{e}^{z}+\operatorname{ln}y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+xy{e}^{z}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+z(x+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$ 
Evaluate $\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1,1,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+R\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf{F}$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F}=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x(y{e}^{z}+\operatorname{ln}y))+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{z})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z(x+1)) \\  & =(y{e}^{z}+\operatorname{ln}y)+x{e}^{z}+(x+1) \\  & =y{e}^{z}+\operatorname{ln}y+x{e}^{z}+x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1,1,0),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathrm{∇}\cdot \mathbf{F})(1,1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{0}+\operatorname{ln}1+1\cdot {e}^{0}+1+1 \\  & =1+0+1+1+1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/e3/e30919dc7cc107bdda9872079b4dc0e59fe8e3e5767aa2d407b9d0af392803e0.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement $\text{div}\,F>0$ is true, whereas statements $\text{div}\,F=0$ and $\text{div}\,F<0$ are false. Notice that the lengths of the vector's $y$-components increase as we move vertically away from the origin. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a source at every point.

- Statement “$F$ is solenoidal” is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{div}\,F>0$ only.

question.:question/problem:

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement $\text{div}\,F=0$ is true, whereas statements $\text{div}\,F>0$ and $\text{div}\,F<0$ are false. For any point $P,$ the sum of the inward-pointing vectors equals the sum of the outward-pointing vectors. Therefore, $F$ acts neither like a source nor a sink.

- Statement “$F$ is solenoidal” is true. Since $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere, the vector field $F$ is solenoidal.

question.:question/problem: Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=x{e}^{yz}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+yz\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{e}^{yz}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ what is $\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+R\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the curl of $\mathbf{F}$ is the vector field given by

$$
curl\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}=\mathrm{∇}\times \mathbf{F}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{vmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ x{e}^{yz} & yz & {e}^{yz}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{yz})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz)]\mathbf{i}-[\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{yz})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{yz})]\mathbf{j}+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{yz})]\mathbf{k} \\  & =(z{e}^{yz}-y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-(0-xy{e}^{yz})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(0-xz{e}^{yz})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(z{e}^{yz}-y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+xy{e}^{yz}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-xz{e}^{yz}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=({y}^{2}+{e}^{x})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}(xy)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ what is the scalar curl of $\mathbf{F}?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $\mathbf{F}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))-\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+{e}^{x}) \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-2y \\  & =y(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-2).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=({x}^{2}+xy)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{ln}(x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf{F}$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $\mathbf{F}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))-\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+y}-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(\frac{1}{2},0),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(1/2,0)} & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2}+0)}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =2-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/17/1709a94b7361a1e8764d94199f9e84802ae925a09e6481250d0846b83bb6549f.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

![](images/7c/7c831425eae7afd709d546a8e05100f495adc04bba6450cfa56d370b415a28f5.png)

If $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$ is true, whereas statement $\text{curl}\,F=0$ is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would rotate clockwise. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- Statement “$\text{curl}\,F$ points in the negative $z$-direction” is true. Using our right hand, if we wrap our fingers in the direction of rotation (clockwise), our thumb will point into the screen. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F$ also points into from the screen, in the direction of decreasing $z.$

- Statement “$F$ is irrotational” is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not irrotational.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$; “$\text{curl}\,F$ points in the negative $z$-direction” only.

question.:question/problem:

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

question.:question/worked-solution:

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. - If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

![](images/97/979b63f21e56924bd7880f9487cf829089e38cf14d287e70196c7a661e41f97f.png)

Moreover, if $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement $\text{curl}\,F=0$ is true, whereas statement $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$ is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would not rotate. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

- Statement “$F$ is irrotational” is true. Since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ the vector field $F$ is irrotational.

- Statement “$\text{curl}\,F$ points in the negative $z$-direction” is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F=0,$ it points in neither the positive nor the negative $z$-direction.

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}+5\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=-\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}.$ Determine $\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:

$$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $y={x}^{3}$ between the points $(0,0)$ and $(2,8)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)={t}^{3}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,{t}^{3}⟩,\hspace{2em}0\le t\le 2
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+3{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+9{t}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =t\cdot {t}^{3}={t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{4}\sqrt{1+9{t}^{4}}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}2{x}^{3}y\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $y=\frac{1}{x}$ between the points $(1,1)$ and $(2,\frac{1}{2})?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=\frac{1}{t}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\frac{1}{t}⟩,\hspace{2em}1\le t\le 2
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{\left(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+1}}{{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2{x}^{3}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =2\cdot {t}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{t}=2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2{t}^{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{{t}^{4}+1}}{{t}^{2}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{t}^{4}+1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=2xy$ along the curve $y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}},$ $\,0\le x\le 2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}⟩,\hspace{2em}0\le t\le 2
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}})\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}-\frac{t}{\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{\left(-\frac{t}{\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4-{t}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =2t\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2t\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}\cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{t}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =2{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2({2}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ along the line $y=x,$ $\,0\le x\le 3.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=t.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}t⟩,\hspace{2em}0\le t\le 3
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =t+t=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2t\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}\hspace{0.167em}{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\sqrt{2}({3}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =9\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=({x}^{2}+y)$ along the line $y=3x+2,$ $\,0\le x\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=3t+2.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}3t+2⟩,\hspace{2em}0\le t\le 1
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+2)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & ={t}^{2}+(3t+2)={t}^{2}+3t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+3t+2)\cdot \sqrt{10}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+3t+2)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{10}\hspace{0.167em}(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}+\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}+2t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{10}(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{3}{2}+2) \\  & =\frac{23\sqrt{10}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{x-y}$ along the line $y=x-4,$ $\,0\le x\le 2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=t-4.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}t-4⟩,\hspace{2em}0\le t\le 2
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-4)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{x-y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{1}{t-(t-4))}=\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\hspace{0.167em}t\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}(2-0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}(2t),\hspace{1em}y={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(t),\hspace{2em}0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,{y}^{′}(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =-\,\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{2\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =-\,\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =-\,\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x={e}^{1/t},\,y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-1}},\,1<t<\infty ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}{e}^{1/t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=-\frac{t}{({t}^{2}-1)^{3/2}}.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{\left(-\frac{t}{({t}^{2}-1)^{3/2}}\right)}{(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}{e}^{1/t})} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{3}{e}^{-1/t}}{({t}^{2}-1)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{2}^{3}{e}^{-1/2}}{({2}^{2}-1)^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{8}{{3}^{3/2}\sqrt{e}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{27e}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{t})},\,y=\operatorname{cot}⁡({e}^{t}),\,-\infty <t<1,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}({e}^{t})}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}({e}^{t})\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}({e}^{t})}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}({e}^{t})}}, \\ {y}^{'}(t) & =-{e}^{t}{\operatorname{csc}}^{2}({e}^{t}).\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =\frac{-{e}^{t}{\operatorname{csc}}^{2}({e}^{t})}{\left(\frac{{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}({e}^{t})}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}({e}^{t})}}\right)} \\  & =-\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}({e}^{t})}}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}({e}^{t})\operatorname{cos}({e}^{t})} \\  & =-\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{3/2}({e}^{t})\operatorname{cos}({e}^{t})}\hspace{0.167em}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right),$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & =-\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{3/2}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)} \\  & =-\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2}{{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{3/2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)} \\  & =-2\cdot {2}^{3/2}\hspace{0.167em}\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =-8\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\hspace{0.167em}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\frac{1}{3},\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ on the curve. Determine the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $x$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+\frac{1}{3}=1+0+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{4}{3}, \\ y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+1=0+1=1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(\frac{4}{3},1).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\right) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi /2} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-0} \\  & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\frac{4}{3},1)$ and the slope $m=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =1\cdot (x-\frac{4}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $x$-axis when $y=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0-1 & =1\cdot (x-\frac{4}{3}) \\ -1 & =x-\frac{4}{3} \\ x & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(\frac{1}{3},\,0)$ is the $x$-intercept.

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically by

$$
x=5-t,\,\,\,y={t}^{2}-1,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=5-t\,⇒\,t=5-x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=5-x$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(5-x)^{2}-1 \\  & =25-10x+{x}^{2}-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-10x+24\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y={x}^{2}-10x+24.$

Finally, since $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $x=5-t,$ we must have $x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

So, the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y={x}^{2}-10x+24,\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\sqrt{t}\,⇒\,t={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t={x}^{2}$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={x}^{2}(9-{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y={x}^{2}(9-{x}^{2}).$

Finally, since $t\ge 0$ and $x=\sqrt{t},$ we must have $x\ge 0.$

So, the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y={x}^{2}(9-{x}^{2}),\,x\ge 0.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3,\,\,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=x+3 \\ y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t=y.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Pythagorean identity ${\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t=1$, we get

$$
(x+3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $(x+3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically by

$$
x=\frac{1}{t+1},\,\,\,y=\frac{1}{t-2},\,t\ne -1,\,2.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{t+1}\,⇒\,t=\frac{1}{x}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now substituting $t=\frac{1}{x}-1$ into our expression for $y$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{((\frac{1}{x}-1)-2)} \\ y & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{x}-3)} \\ y & =\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1-3x}{x}\right)} \\ y & =\frac{x}{1-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=\frac{x}{1-3x}.$

Finally, since $t\ne -1,\,2$ and $x=\frac{1}{t+1},$ we must have $x\ne 0,\,\frac{1}{3}.$

So, the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y=\frac{x}{1-3x},\,x\ne 0,\,\frac{1}{3}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2,\,\,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t=x+2 \\ y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=y-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Pythagorean identity ${\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t=1,$ we get

$$
(y-3)^{2}+(x+2)^{2}=1.
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $(y-3)^{2}+(x+2)^{2}=1.$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\,\,y=\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,0<t<\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=x \\ y=\operatorname{tan}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t=y\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Pythagorean identity ${\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t=1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t & =1 \\ {\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t & =1-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t \\ \operatorname{cos}t & =\sqrt{1-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We used here that $\operatorname{cos}⁡t>0$ in the range $0<t<\frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, using the definition of a tangent, we obtain

$$
\operatorname{tan}t=\frac{\operatorname{sin}t}{\operatorname{cos}t}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}t}{\sqrt{1-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}}.
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=x$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡t=y$ into this formula, we get

$$
y=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=3\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,\,\,y=\operatorname{csc}⁡t,\,t\in (0,\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=3\operatorname{cot}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cot}⁡t=\frac{x}{3} \\ y=\operatorname{csc}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{csc}⁡t=y.\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the Pythagorean identity ${\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t=1$ by ${\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}+\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t} & =\frac{1}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t} \\ 1+{\left(\frac{\operatorname{cos}t}{\operatorname{sin}t}\right)}^{2} & ={\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}t}\right)}^{2} \\ 1+{\operatorname{cot}}^{2}t & ={\operatorname{csc}}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cot}⁡t=\frac{x}{3}$ and $\operatorname{csc}⁡t=y$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)}^{2}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is ${y}^{2}=1+{\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)}^{2}.$

question.:question/problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(2\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2} \\  & =4{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(2\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2} \\  & =4{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +4{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  \\  & =4({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta ) \\  & =4(1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$

question.:question/problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1,\,y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 2(x-1) & =\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 4(x-1)^{2} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ 2(y-2) & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  \\ 4(y-2)^{2} & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-1)^{2}+4(y-2)^{2} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  \\ 4(x-1)^{2}+4(y-2)^{2} & =1 \\ (x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the Cartesian equation of the circle is $(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$

question.:question/problem:

First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta $ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}\theta }3r\operatorname{cos}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}\theta {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}\theta }r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}\theta \hspace{0.222em}{[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}\theta \hspace{0.222em}(\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta }{2}-0)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{3}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate with respect to $\theta :$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{3}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}\theta (1-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{[\operatorname{sin}\theta -\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[(\operatorname{sin}\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{1}{3}{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}\frac{\pi }{2})-(\operatorname{sin}0-\frac{1}{3}{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}0)] \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[(1-\frac{1}{3})-0] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Integrate the function $f(x,y)=15{x}^{2}y$ over the disk of radius $1$ centered at the origin.

question.:question/problem: Integrate the function $f(x,y)=4{y}^{2}$ over the disk of radius $3$ centered at the origin.

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4{y}^{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}4(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2}\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}4{r}^{3}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}4{r}^{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta \hspace{0.222em}{[{r}^{4}]}_{0}^{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta (81-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =81{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =81{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}2\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{2}{[\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{81}{2}[(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}4\pi -\operatorname{sin}0)] \\  & =\frac{81}{2}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =81\pi .\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(0,1).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x=\sqrt{2y-{y}^{2}}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{2y-{y}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2} & =2y-{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2y \\ (r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2} & =2r\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta ) & =2r\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =2r\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{sin}\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{sin}\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x}{y}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}\frac{r\operatorname{cos}\theta }{r\operatorname{sin}\theta }\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}\theta }r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}\theta }\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }(2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta -0)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}2\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}2\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}\pi -\operatorname{cos}0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-1-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =2 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}\theta +1)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta -1)^{2} & =2 \\ {r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +2r\operatorname{cos}\theta -2r\operatorname{sin}\theta +2 & =2 \\ {r}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )-2r(\operatorname{sin}\theta -\operatorname{cos}\theta ) & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r(\operatorname{sin}\theta -\operatorname{cos}\theta ) & =0 \\ r(r-2(\operatorname{sin}\theta -\operatorname{cos}\theta )) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ).$

- For $y=x+2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x+2 \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2 \\ r(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =2 \\ r & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents the half-annulus between the disks of radii $3$ and $5$ centered at the origin. 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ we obtain $r=3.$

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25,$ we obtain $r=5.$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ The entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\pi ,$ as depicted below.  

![](images/da/da18aafec278b5d44b0530097729e4cb4b319e219c005fc155d78fab8aa90937.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta )\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}3\le r\le 5,\hspace{0.222em}0\le \theta <\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}\frac{{r}^{3}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta }{\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2}}}\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{3}^{5}\frac{{r}^{3}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta }{r}\cdot r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{3}^{5}{r}^{3}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta {[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{3}^{5}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta (\frac{625}{4}-\frac{81}{4})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =136{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =136{[-\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{3}\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =136\cdot (\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{272}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}-y,\hspace{0.222em}2x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=3x-2y$ for $0\le x\le 5$ and $-3\le y\le 3.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={\int }_{0}^{5}{\int }_{-3}^{3}\enclose{box}{\phantom{AAAAAAA}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}v,\hspace{0.222em}3u-2v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 5,\,-3\le v\le 3\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}3⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(3u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}-y,\hspace{0.222em}2x⟩{|}_{x=u,\hspace{0.167em}\,y=v,\hspace{0.167em}\,z=3u-2v} \\  & =⟨3u-2v,\hspace{0.222em}-v,\hspace{0.222em}2u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨3u-2v,\hspace{0.222em}-v,\hspace{0.222em}2u⟩\cdot ⟨-3,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\  & =(3u-2v)\cdot (-3)+(-v)\cdot (2)+2u\cdot 1 \\  & =-9u+6v-2v+2u \\  & =-7u+4v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}-y,\hspace{0.222em}2x⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-7u+4v)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{\int }_{-3}^{3}({\color{blue}-7u+4v})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨-x,\hspace{0.222em}-y,\hspace{0.222em}xyz⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=2x+y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨-x,\hspace{0.222em}-y,\hspace{0.222em}xyz⟩{|}_{z=2x+y} \\  & =⟨-x,\hspace{0.222em}-y,\hspace{0.222em}xy(2x+y)⟩ \\  & =⟨\underbrace{-x}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{-y}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{xy(2x+y)}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-x,\hspace{0.222em}-y,\hspace{0.222em}xyz⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-x)\cdot 2-(-y)\cdot (1)+xy(2x+y))\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2xy+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{x{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+\frac{1}{2}+{x}^{2}+\frac{x}{3})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{7x}{3}+\frac{1}{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{7{x}^{2}}{6}+\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{6}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨xy,\hspace{0.222em}x+y,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{z}⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨xy,\hspace{0.222em}x+y,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{z}⟩{|}_{z=x+y} \\  & =⟨xy,\hspace{0.222em}x+y,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{x+y}⟩ \\  & =⟨\underbrace{xy}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{x+y}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{{e}^{x+y}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨xy,\hspace{0.222em}x+y,\hspace{0.222em}{e}^{z}⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(xy)\cdot 1-(x+y)\cdot 1+{e}^{x+y})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-xy-x-y+{e}^{x+y})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}(-xy-x-y+{e}^{x+y})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{x{y}^{2}}{2}-xy-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+{e}^{x+y}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}-{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{e}^{2x}-{e}^{x})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}-\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}+{e}^{2x}-{e}^{x})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{{x}^{4}}{8}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{2x}}{2}-{e}^{x}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(-\frac{1}{8}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-e)-(0+\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{2}-8e-1}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨x,\hspace{0.222em}y-z,\hspace{0.222em}x+y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x-2y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $-1\le y\le 1.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\enclose{box}{\phantom{AAAAAAA}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}v,\hspace{0.222em}u-2v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 1\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =⟨x,\hspace{0.222em}y-z,\hspace{0.222em}x+y⟩{|}_{x=u,\hspace{0.167em}\,y=v,\hspace{0.167em}\,z=u-2v} \\  & =⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}v-(u-2v),\hspace{0.222em}u+v⟩ \\  & =⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}3v-u,\hspace{0.222em}u+v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}3v-u,\hspace{0.222em}u+v⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\  & =u\cdot (-1)+(3v-u)\cdot 2+(u+v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-u+6v-2u+u+v \\  & =-2u+7v.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨x,\hspace{0.222em}y-z,\hspace{0.222em}x+y⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2u+7v)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\color{blue}(-2u+7v)}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

For a surface $S$ given by $x=k(y,z)$ for $(y,z)\in D,$ the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{D}(P+\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\frac{∂k}{∂y}-R\frac{∂k}{\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.
$$

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $x=k(y,z),$ it can be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(y,z)=⟨k(y,z),\hspace{0.222em}y,\hspace{0.222em}z⟩.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{y}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂k}{∂y},\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{z}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂k}{∂z},\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{y}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{z}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂k}{∂y} & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{∂k}{∂z} & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}=⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-\frac{∂k}{∂y},\hspace{0.222em}-\frac{∂k}{∂z}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(x,y))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{y}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{z}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩\cdot ⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-\frac{∂k}{∂y},\hspace{0.222em}-\frac{∂k}{∂z}⟩\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(P+({\color{blue}-Q}\hspace{0.167em})\frac{∂k}{∂y}-R\frac{∂k}{{\color{blue}∂z}})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For a surface $S$ given by $y=-{x}^{2}z$ for $(x,z)\in D,$ the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{D}(\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\hspace{0.167em}xz+Q+\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\hspace{0.167em}{x}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.
$$

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?

*Hint: The orientation of $S$ should be chosen such that the unit normal vector has a positive  $\mathbf{j}$-component.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $y=-{x}^{2}z,$ it can be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(x,z)=⟨x,\hspace{0.222em}-{x}^{2}z,z⟩.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'} & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-2xz,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{z}^{'} & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}-{x}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{z}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & -2xz & 0 \\ 0 & -{x}^{2} & 1\end{vmatrix}=⟨-2xz,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}-{x}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

However, notice that the $\mathbf{j}$-component is negative. Therefore, we select the normal vector that points in the *opposite* direction:

$$
{\mathbf{r}}_{z}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'}=-{\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{z}^{'}=⟨2xz,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}{x}^{2}⟩
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(x,z))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{x}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{z}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,R\hspace{0.222em}⟩\cdot ⟨2xz,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}{x}^{2}⟩\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({\color{blue}2P}\hspace{0.167em}xz+Q+{\color{blue}R}\hspace{0.167em}{x}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{D}(P+\bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\hspace{0.167em}z+\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\hspace{0.167em}y)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $x=2yz,$ it can be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(y,z)=⟨2yz,\hspace{0.222em}y,\hspace{0.222em}z⟩.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{y}^{'} & =⟨2z,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{z}^{'} & =⟨2y,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{y}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{z}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2z & 1 & 0 \\ 2y & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}=⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-2z,\hspace{0.222em}-2y⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(y,z))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{y}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{z}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩\cdot ⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-2z,\hspace{0.222em}-2y⟩\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(P+(\hspace{0.167em}{\color{blue}-2Q})\hspace{0.167em}z+(\hspace{0.167em}{\color{blue}-2R})\hspace{0.167em}y\hspace{0.167em})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$
