Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}y+2z,\hspace{0.222em}2x-y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=y-x$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $-1\le y\le 2.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ through $S$ can be expressed as 

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}\enclose{box}{\phantom{AAAAAAA}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨u,\hspace{0.222em}v,\hspace{0.222em}v-u⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,-1\le v\le 2\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}y+2z,\hspace{0.222em}2x-y⟩{|}_{x=u,\hspace{0.167em}\,y=v,\hspace{0.167em}\,z=v-u} \\  & =⟨v-u,\hspace{0.222em}v+2(v-u),\hspace{0.222em}2u-v⟩ \\  & =⟨v-u,\hspace{0.222em}3v-2u,\hspace{0.222em}2u-v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and ${\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}) & =⟨v-u,\hspace{0.222em}3v-2u,\hspace{0.222em}2u-v⟩\cdot ⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}-1,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩ \\  & =(v-u)\cdot 1+(3v-2u)\cdot (-1)+(2u-v)\cdot 1 \\  & =v-u-3v+2u+2u-v \\  & =3u-3v.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z,\hspace{0.222em}y+2z,\hspace{0.222em}2x-y⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v))\cdot ({\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3u-3v)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\color{blue}(3u-3v)}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}v\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}y⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)$ for $-\pi \le x\le 0$ and $-x\le y\le 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y) \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}y⟩{|}_{z=\operatorname{cos}(x+y)} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{1}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{0}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{y}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}y⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}(x+y))-0\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}(x+y))+y)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\operatorname{sin}(x+y)+y)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{0}{\int }_{-x}^{0}(\operatorname{sin}(x+y)+y)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{0}{[-\operatorname{cos}(x+y)+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=-x}^{y=0}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{0}(-\operatorname{cos}x+0)-(-\operatorname{cos}0+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{0}(-\operatorname{cos}x+1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\operatorname{sin}x+x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}]}_{-\pi }^{0} \\  & =0-(-0+(-\pi )-\frac{(-\pi )^{3}}{6}) \\  & =\pi -\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨y,\hspace{0.222em}x+z,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩,
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z={e}^{x}$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x})={e}^{x} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x})=0\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ through $S$ is given by 

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨y,\hspace{0.222em}x+z,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨y,\hspace{0.222em}x+z,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩{|}_{z={e}^{x}} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{y}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{x+{e}^{x}}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{0}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨y,\hspace{0.222em}x+z,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot ({e}^{x})-(x+{e}^{x})\cdot 0+0)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y{e}^{x})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-y{e}^{x})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{[-\frac{{y}^{2}{e}^{x}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{e}^{x}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{[{e}^{x}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-1}-e}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy),\hspace{0.222em}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy),\hspace{0.222em}1⟩,
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=\operatorname{tan}⁡(xy)$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $-x\le y\le 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{tan}(xy))=\frac{y}{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy)} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}(xy))=\frac{x}{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy)}\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ through $S$ is given by 

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy),\hspace{0.222em}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy),\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy),\hspace{0.222em}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy),\hspace{0.222em}1⟩{|}_{z=\operatorname{tan}(xy)} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy)}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy)}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{1}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy),\hspace{0.222em}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy),\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy))\cdot \left(\frac{y}{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy)}\right)-({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy))\cdot \left(\frac{x}{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(xy)}\right)+1)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y-x+1)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-x}^{0}(-y-x+1)\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-xy+y]}_{y=-x}^{y=0}\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-{x}^{2}+x)\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+x)\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\hspace{0.222em}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\hspace{0.222em}{z}^{2}+1⟩,
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=2\sqrt{xy}$ for $3\le x\le 4$ and $1\le y\le 2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\sqrt{xy})=\sqrt{\frac{y}{x}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\sqrt{xy})=\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ through $S$ is given by 

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\hspace{0.222em}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\hspace{0.222em}{z}^{2}+1⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\hspace{0.222em}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\hspace{0.222em}{z}^{2}+1⟩{|}_{z=2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{4xy+1}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\hspace{0.222em}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\hspace{0.222em}{z}^{2}+1⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{y}{x}}-\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}+4xy+1)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1-\frac{x}{y}+4xy+1)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{x}{y}+4xy)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}{\int }_{1}^{2}(-\frac{x}{y}+4xy)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}{[-x\operatorname{ln}y+2x{y}^{2}]}_{y=1}^{y=2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}(-x\operatorname{ln}2+8x+0-2x)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}(6-\operatorname{ln}2)x\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & =(6-\operatorname{ln}2){[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{3}^{4} \\  & =\frac{7(6-\operatorname{ln}2)}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}

In this case, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ through $S$ is given by 

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨x+y,\hspace{0.222em}y-x,\hspace{0.222em}z⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨x+y,\hspace{0.222em}y-x,\hspace{0.222em}z⟩{|}_{z=1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{x+y}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{y-x}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨3{x}^{3}y,\hspace{0.222em}2yz,\hspace{0.222em}2x(y+z)⟩,
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=2x+y$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=⟨P,\hspace{0.222em}Q,\hspace{0.222em}R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ through $S$ is given by 

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨3{x}^{3}y,\hspace{0.222em}2yz,\hspace{0.222em}2x(y+z)⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨3{x}^{3}y,\hspace{0.222em}2yz,\hspace{0.222em}2xz⟩{|}_{z=2x+y} \\ \mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨3{x}^{3}y,\hspace{0.222em}2y(2x+y),\hspace{0.222em}2x(y+2x+y)⟩{|}_{z=2x+y} \\  & =⟨\underbrace{3{x}^{3}y}_{P},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{4xy+2{y}^{2}}_{Q},\hspace{0.222em}\underbrace{4xy+4{x}^{2}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨3{x}^{3}y,\hspace{0.222em}2yz,\hspace{0.222em}2x(y+z)⟩\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(3{x}^{3}y)\cdot (2)-(4xy+2{y}^{2})\cdot (1)+4xy+4{x}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-6{x}^{3}y-2{y}^{2}+4{x}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-6{x}^{3}y-2{y}^{2}+4{x}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[-3{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}+4{x}^{2}y]}_{0}^{1}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{x}^{3}-\frac{2}{3}+4{x}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{3{x}^{4}}{4}-\frac{2x}{3}+\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-12-\frac{4}{3}+\frac{32}{3} \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

To find the range of $x,$ we can start by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={t}^{2}-2t \\  & ={(t-1)}^{2}-{(1)}^{2} \\  & ={(t-1)}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x=5t-{t}^{2},\,\,\,y={t}^{2},\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

determine the ranges of $x$ and $y.$

Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ we can start by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5t-{t}^{2} \\  & =-({t}^{2}-5t) \\  & =-{(t-\frac{5}{2})}^{2}+{\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)}^{2} \\  & =-{(t-\frac{5}{2})}^{2}+\frac{25}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${(t-\frac{5}{2})}^{2}\ge 0,$ we can conclude that $x\le \frac{25}{4}.$

- To find the range of $y,$ notice that ${t}^{2}\ge 0$ for all $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Consequently, $y\ge 0.$

Therefore, the ranges are $x\le \frac{25}{4}$ and $y\ge 0.$

question.:question/problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=1,$ $x=e,$ $y=0,$ $y=2,$ $z=0,$ $z=2.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $\mathbf{F}=y\operatorname{ln}x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{z}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(x-{y}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ find the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}={∭}_{R}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x-{y}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{y}{x}+0+0 \\  & =\frac{y}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∭}_{R}\frac{y}{x}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{y}{x}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}z\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}y\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}z \\  & =[\operatorname{ln}x]_{x=1}^{x=e}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\cdot [z]_{z=0}^{z=2} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}e-\operatorname{ln}1)\cdot (\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2})\cdot (2-0) \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (2-0)\cdot (2-0) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=0,$ $x=1,$ $y=1,$ $y=2,$ $z=1,$ $z=3.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $\mathbf{F}={x}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(x+{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ find the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}={∭}_{R}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+{y}^{2}) \\  & =2x+2+0 \\  & =2x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∭}_{R}(2x+2)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}(2x+2)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}z\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+2)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{1}^{2}\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{1}^{3}\text{d}z \\  & =[{x}^{2}+2x]_{x=0}^{x=1}\cdot (2-1)\cdot (3-1) \\  & =({1}^{2}+2(1)-0)\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=0,$ $x=1,$ $y=1,$ $y=2,$ $z=-1,$ $z=1.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $\mathbf{F}=2y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x{y}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2xyz\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ find the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}={∭}_{R}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2xyz) \\  & =0+2xy+2xy \\  & =4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∭}_{R}4xy\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}4xy\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}z\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2x\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{1}^{2}2y\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}z \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=1}\cdot [{y}^{2}]_{y=1}^{y=2}\cdot (1-(-1)) \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (4-1)\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,x={t}^{2},$ and $y=t,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/f0/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2t,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot 2t+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\cdot 1 \\  & =2t\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡({t}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)$ and $y={x}^{2}+1,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2x({x}^{2}+1)}{{x}^{2}+1}=2x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2x \\  & =2x(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=xy,$ where $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂t}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}t(-\operatorname{sin}t)+(\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}s)\cdot \operatorname{cos}t \\  & =-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+\operatorname{sin}s\operatorname{cos}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=y{e}^{x},$ where $x=t+s$ and $y=ts.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =ts{e}^{t+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{t+s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(ts{e}^{t+s})(1)+({e}^{t+s})(t) \\  & =t{e}^{t+s}(s+1).\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/b5/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y+z}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{s+t}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{1}{s+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}+{t}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}\cdot (1)+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{s+t}\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{-({s}^{2}+{t}^{2})+2t(s+t)}{(s+t)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2ts-{s}^{2}}{(s+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${c}_{1}=-1,$ ${c}_{2}=2$ and ${c}_{3}=1,$ and therefore

$$
{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+{c}_{3}=-1+2+1=2.
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨-2,0,1⟩$, $\mathbf{b}=⟨5,2,-4⟩$ and $\mathbf{c}=⟨1,0,3⟩.$ Find $\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the scalar triple product $\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 0 & 1 \\ 5 & 2 & -4 \\ 1 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-2)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix}-0\cdot \begin{vmatrix}5 & -4 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}+1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}5 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-2(2\cdot 3-(-4)\cdot 0)-0+(5\cdot 0-2\cdot 1) \\  & =-12-0-2 \\  & =-14.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\mathbf{b}\cdot (\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{c})$, if $4\mathbf{a}\cdot (-\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})=12.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we factor out the constants and get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\mathbf{a}\cdot (-\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =12 \\ 4\cdot (-1)\cdot [\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})] & =12 \\ \mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}\cdot (\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{c}) & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨2,3,0⟩$ and $\mathbf{b}=⟨6,4,0⟩.$ Find $\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 4\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(3\cdot 0-4\cdot 0)\mathbf{i}-(2\cdot 0-6\cdot 0)\mathbf{j}+(2\cdot 4-6\cdot 3)\mathbf{k} \\  & =(0)\mathbf{i}-(0)\mathbf{j}+(8-18)\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨0,0,-10⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨0,0,3⟩$ and $\mathbf{b}=⟨2,0,1⟩.$ Find $\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((0)(1)-(0)(3))\mathbf{i}-((0)(1)-(2)(3))\mathbf{j}+((0)(0)-(2)(0))\mathbf{k} \\  & =(0-0)\mathbf{i}-(0-6)\mathbf{j}+(0-0)\mathbf{k} \\  & =6\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨x,2,3⟩$, $\mathbf{b}=⟨2x,5,2⟩$ and $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|=\sqrt{393}.$ Find $x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ x & 2 & 3 \\ 2x & 5 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 5 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}x & 3 \\ 2x & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}x & 2 \\ 2x & 5\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(4-15)\mathbf{i}-(2x-6x)\mathbf{j}+(5x-4x)\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-11,4x,x⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{(-11)^{2}+(4x)^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{121+16{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{17{x}^{2}+121}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we solve for $x$ the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{393} \\ \sqrt{17{x}^{2}+121} & =\sqrt{393} \\ 17{x}^{2}+121 & =393 \\ 17{x}^{2} & =272 \\ {x}^{2} & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\pm 4.$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨1,5,4⟩$ and $\mathbf{b}=⟨2,3,0⟩.$ Find $\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 5 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}5 & 4 \\ 3 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((5)(0)-(3)(4))\mathbf{i}-((1)(0)-(2)(4))\mathbf{j}+((1)(3)-(2)(5))\mathbf{k} \\  & =(0-12)\mathbf{i}-(0-8)\mathbf{j}+(3-10)\mathbf{k} \\  & =-12\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j}-7\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨-2,2,0⟩$ and $\mathbf{b}=⟨0,2,-3⟩.$ Find $\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & -3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((2)(-3)-(2)(0))\mathbf{i}-((-2)(-3)-(0)(0))\mathbf{j}+((-2)(2)-(0)(2))\mathbf{k} \\  & =(-6-0)\mathbf{i}-(6-0)\mathbf{j}+(-4-0)\mathbf{k} \\  & =-6\mathbf{i}-6\mathbf{j}-4\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨1,3,2⟩$, $\mathbf{b}=⟨3,4,1⟩$ and $\mathbf{c}=⟨2,0,1⟩.$ Find $\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the scalar triple product $\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}-3\cdot \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}+2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}3 & 4 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4\cdot 1-0\cdot 1)-3(3\cdot 1-2\cdot 1)+2(3\cdot 0-2\cdot 4) \\  & =4-3-16 \\  & =-15.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨1,-1,2⟩$, $\mathbf{b}=⟨2,0,3⟩$ and $\mathbf{c}=⟨2,4,2⟩.$ Find $\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the scalar triple product $\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 4 & 2\end{vmatrix}-(-1)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix}+2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(0\cdot 2-4\cdot 3)+(2\cdot 2-2\cdot 3)+2(2\cdot 4-2\cdot 0) \\  & =-12-2+16 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\mathbf{b}\cdot (\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{c})$, if $3\mathbf{a}\cdot (2\mathbf{b}\times (-\mathbf{c}))=8.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we factor out the constants and get

$$

question.:question/problem:

The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\,\,y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{2} \\ y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using double angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}2t & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t \\  & =(1-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t)-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t \\  & =1-2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{2}$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{3} & =1-2{\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}^{2} \\ \frac{y}{3} & =1-2\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\right) \\ \frac{y}{3} & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2} \\ y & =3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\,\,y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t=\frac{x}{4} \\ y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using double angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}2t & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t \\  & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-(1-{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t) \\  & =2{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡t=\frac{x}{4}$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{2}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{2} & =2{\left(\frac{x}{4}\right)}^{2}-1 \\ \frac{y}{2} & =2\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}\right)-1 \\ \frac{y}{2} & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-1 \\ y & =2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-1).$

$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=-5+\frac{5{x}^{2}}{18}.$

To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =7\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ \frac{(x+5)^{2}}{{7}^{2}} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta  \\ \frac{{(x+5)}^{2}}{49} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-13 & =7\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ \frac{(y-13)^{2}}{{7}^{2}} & =\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ \frac{{(y-13)}^{2}}{49} & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(x+5)}^{2}}{49}+\frac{{(y-13)}^{2}}{49} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  \\ \frac{{(x+5)}^{2}}{49}+\frac{{(y-13)}^{2}}{49} & =1 \\ {(x+5)}^{2}+{(y-13)}^{2} & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian equation is ${(x+5)}^{2}+{(y-13)}^{2}=49.$

$$

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{2}

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the level curve that passes through the point $Q(1,1)$ for the function $f(x,y)=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $Q$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1) & =\frac{2(1)}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the level curve that passes through $Q(1,1)$ is the $1$-level curve.

Recall that the level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=1.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ \frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =1 \\ 2y & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2y+1 & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level curve that passes through $Q(1,1)$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1.$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y-5yz,$ where $x=st,$ $y={s}^{3}$ and $z=s\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}-5z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-5y.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(st)({s}^{3})=2{s}^{4}t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(st)^{2}-5(s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)={s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =-5{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2{s}^{4}t)\cdot t+({s}^{2}{t}^{2}-5s\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3{s}^{2}+(-5{s}^{3})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}+3{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-15{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-5{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =5{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-20{s}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-2y,$ where $x=s{t}^{2}$ and $y={s}^{3}-t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy-2\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =({s}^{3}-t)^{2}={s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(s{t}^{2})({s}^{3}-t)-2=2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & ={t}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =3{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =({s}^{6}-2{s}^{3}t+{t}^{2})({t}^{2})+(2{s}^{4}{t}^{2}-2s{t}^{3}-2)(3{s}^{2}) \\  & ={s}^{6}{t}^{2}-2{s}^{3}{t}^{3}+{t}^{4}+6{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-6{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2} \\  & =7{s}^{6}{t}^{2}-8{s}^{3}{t}^{3}-6{s}^{2}+{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Simplify $$
\displaystyle \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }+\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}\theta }+\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta }{(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )\operatorname{cos}\theta }+\frac{(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}\theta (1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )} \\  & =\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )}^{2}}{(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )\operatorname{cos}\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )}^{2}}{(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )\operatorname{cos}\theta } & =\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +1-2\operatorname{sin}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }{(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )\operatorname{cos}\theta } \\  & =\frac{({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta )+1-2\operatorname{sin}\theta }{(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )\operatorname{cos}\theta } \\  & =\frac{1+1-2\operatorname{sin}\theta }{(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )\operatorname{cos}\theta } \\  & =\frac{2-2\operatorname{sin}\theta }{(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )\operatorname{cos}\theta } \\  & =\frac{2(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )}{(1-\operatorname{sin}\theta )\operatorname{cos}\theta } \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{cos}\theta } \\  & =2\operatorname{sec}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }+\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }=2\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .
$$

$$

First, we expand the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}t(\frac{\operatorname{cos}t}{\operatorname{sin}t}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}t}{\operatorname{cos}t}) & =\operatorname{sin}t\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}t}{\operatorname{sin}t}+\operatorname{sin}t\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}t}{\operatorname{cos}t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}t\cdot \operatorname{sin}t}{\operatorname{sin}t}+\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{\operatorname{cos}t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}t\cdot \enclose{updiagonalstrike}{\operatorname{sin}t}}{\enclose{updiagonalstrike}{\operatorname{sin}t}}+\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{\operatorname{cos}t} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}t+\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{\operatorname{cos}t}\end{aligned}
$$

We put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}\theta +\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{\operatorname{cos}t} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}t}{1}+\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{\operatorname{cos}t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}t\cdot \operatorname{cos}t}{1\cdot \operatorname{cos}t}+\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{\operatorname{cos}t} \\  & =\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{\operatorname{cos}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify using the Pythagorean identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{\operatorname{cos}t} &=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}t}=\operatorname{sec}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡t(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t})=\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x)={(5-3x)}^{4},$ find the equation of the tangent at point $(2,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule to find $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$

First, we express $f(x)$ as a composite function:

$$
f={g}^{4},\,g=5-3x
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=4{g}^{3},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

Multiplying the two together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =4{g}^{3}\cdot (-3) \\  & =-12(5-3x)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line at the point where $x=2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & =-12{(5-3(2))}^{3} \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the slope of the tangent line at the point $(2,1)$ is $m=12.$ Now, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =12(x-2) \\ y-1 & =12x-24 \\ y & =12x-23\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression $\operatorname{sin}\theta {\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}\theta .$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we factor $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ from the expression:

$$
\operatorname{sin}\theta {\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}\theta =\operatorname{sin}\theta \cdot ({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta )
$$

Then, we use ${\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta =1$ to simplify the expression in the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}\theta \cdot ({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta +{cos}^{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}\theta \cdot 1 \\  & =\operatorname{sin}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that

$$
\operatorname{sin}\theta {\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}\theta =\operatorname{sin}\theta .
$$

question.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression $\operatorname{sin}x{\operatorname{cos}}^{3}x+{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}x\operatorname{cos}x.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x\cdot ({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x) & =\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x\cdot 1 \\  & =\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x\end{aligned}

We conclude that

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression ${\operatorname{sin}}^{5}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}x.$

question.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression ${\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{4}x+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x\cdot ({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x)+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x\cdot 1+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x \\  & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that

$$
{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{4}x+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x=1.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Simplify the trigonometric expression $$
\frac{\operatorname{sin}t{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}t}{\operatorname{cos}t}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we factor the numerator:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sin}t{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}t}{\operatorname{cos}t}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}t\cdot ({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t)}{\operatorname{cos}t}
$$

Next, we use the Pythagorean identity to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, and then we simplify the resulting expression as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}t\cdot ({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t)}{\operatorname{cos}t} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}t\cdot 1}{\operatorname{cos}t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}t}{\operatorname{cos}t} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}t\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that

$$
\frac{\operatorname{sin}t{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}t}{\operatorname{cos}t}=\operatorname{tan}t.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically by

$$
x={t}^{2}+5,\,\,\,y=\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,t\ne 0.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for ${t}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x={t}^{2}+5\,⇒\,{t}^{2}=x-5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting ${t}^{2}=x-5$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{x-5}\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=\frac{1}{x-5}.$

Finally, since $t\ne 0$ and $x={t}^{2}+5,$ we must have $x\ne 5.$ 

So, the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y=\frac{1}{x-5},\,x\ne 5.
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
x=\sqrt{{t}^{2}-4},\,\,\,y=2{t}^{2},\,t\ge 2.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation, we eliminate $t.$ First, we use the $x$ equation to solve for ${t}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\sqrt{{t}^{2}-4}\,⇒\,{t}^{2}={x}^{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting ${t}^{2}={x}^{2}+4$ into our expression for $y,$ we get

$$
y=2({x}^{2}+4)=2{x}^{2}+8
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=2{x}^{2}+8.$

Finally, since $t\ge 2.$ and $x=\sqrt{{t}^{2}-4},$ we must have $x\ge 0.$

So, the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y=2{x}^{2}+8,\,x\ge 0.
$$

\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

{x}^{′}(t)=5{t}^{4}-2,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-3{t}^{2}.

Therefore,

$$

At the point where $t=-1$ we have

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{3}-3t,\,y=2-t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=0$ on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=0$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={0}^{3}-3\cdot 0=0-0=0, \\ y & =2-0=2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $(0,2).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}-3,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-1.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{3{t}^{2}-3} \\  & =-\,\frac{1}{3{t}^{2}-3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=0,$  the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=0} & =-\,\frac{1}{3\cdot {0}^{2}-3} \\  & =-\,\frac{1}{0-3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\,}=-3
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,2)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=-3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-3(x-0) \\ y & =-3x+2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For a $2\times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

question.:question/problem:
If
$$
\displaystyle S=\begin{bmatrix}1-p & 1+p \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$
and $det(S)=2$, what is the value of $p?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a $2\times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{vmatrix}=ad-bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(S) & =\begin{vmatrix}1-p & 1+p \\ -3 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1-p)\cdot 2-(1+p)\cdot (-3) \\  & =2-2p+3+3p \\  & =5+p\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(S)=2$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(S) & =2 \\ 5+p & =2 \\ p & =2-5 \\ p & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +5,\,\,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -7,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,
$$

determine the ranges of $x$ and $y.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ notice that for $0\le \theta <2\pi ,$ we have $-1\le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ -1+5 & \le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +5\le 1+5 \\ 4 & \le x\le 6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $4\le x\le 6.$

- To find the range of $y,$ notice that for $0\le \theta <2\pi ,$ we have $-1\le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ -6 & \le 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 6 \\ -6-7 & \le 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -7\le 6-7 \\ -13 & \le y\le -1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $-13\le y\le -1.$

Therefore, the ranges are $4\le x\le 6$ and $-13\le y\le -1.$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the level curve that passes through the point $R(3,2)$ for the function $f(x,y)=20-{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $R$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,2) & =20-(3)^{2}-2(2)^{2}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the level curve that passes through $R(3,2)$ is the $3$-level curve.

Recall that the level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=3.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ 20-{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2} & =3 \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2} & =17\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level curve that passes through $R(3,2)$ is the ellipse ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=17.$

question.:question/problem: Find the equation of the level curve that passes through the point $V(2,2)$ for the function $f(x,y)=\frac{8y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $V$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2) & =\frac{8(2)}{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the level curve that passes through $V(2,2)$ is the $2$-level curve.

Recall that the level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ \frac{8y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =2 \\ 4y & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4y+4 & =4 \\ {x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level curve that passes through $V(2,2)$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=4.$

question.:question/problem:
For the function $f(x,y)=\frac{2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4}{{y}^{2}}$, clear the denominator in $f(x,y)=c$ and classify the resulting conic equation in the entire $xy$-plane, including points excluded from the function's domain. Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4}{{y}^{2}} & =c \\ 2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4 & =c{y}^{2} \\ 2{x}^{2}+(3-c){y}^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=3$ then the level curves are $x=\pm \sqrt{2},$ which consists of two vertical lines.

- If $c=0$ then the level curve is $2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=4,$ which is an ellipse.

- If $c=1$ then the level curve is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2,$ which is a circle.

So, only statements “$c=0$ gives an ellipse” and “$c=1$ gives a circle” are true.

question.:question/problem:
The level curves of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}}$ are given by $f(x,y)=c.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}} & =c \\ {x}^{2}-2{y}^{2} & ={c}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=1$ then the level curve is ${x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}=1,$ which is not a line.

- If $c=2$ then the level curve is ${x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}=4,$ which is a hyperbola.

- If $c=0$ then the level curve is $y=\pm \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}},$ which consists of two lines.

So, only statements “$c=2$ gives a hyperbola” and “$c=0$ gives two lines” are true.

question.:question/problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression $\operatorname{sin}x+2{\operatorname{cos}}^{3}x+2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x\operatorname{cos}x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we factor the expression:

$$
\operatorname{sin}x+2{\operatorname{cos}}^{3}x+2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x\operatorname{cos}x=\operatorname{sin}x+2\operatorname{cos}x({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x)
$$

Then, we use ${\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x=1$ to simplify the expression in the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}x+2\operatorname{cos}x({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x) & =\operatorname{sin}x+2\operatorname{cos}x\cdot 1 \\  & =\operatorname{sin}x+2\operatorname{cos}x\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that

$$
\operatorname{sin}x+2{\operatorname{cos}}^{3}x+2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x\operatorname{cos}x=\operatorname{sin}x+2\operatorname{cos}x.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Simplify the trigonometric expression $$
\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}x+\operatorname{sin}x{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+1}{\operatorname{cos}x}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we factor $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ from the first two terms:

$$
\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}x+\operatorname{sin}x{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+1}{\operatorname{cos}x}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}x({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x)+1}{\operatorname{cos}x}
$$

Next, we use the Pythagorean identity to rewrite the expression in the parentheses, and then we simplify the resulting expression as much as possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}x({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x)+1}{\operatorname{cos}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}x+1}{\operatorname{cos}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}x} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}x+\operatorname{sec}x\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that:

$$
\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}x+\operatorname{sin}x{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+1}{\operatorname{cos}x}=\operatorname{tan}x+\operatorname{sec}x
$$

question.:question/problem:
Simplify the trigonometric expression $$
\displaystyle \frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the second term using the definition of $\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$ This gives:

$$
\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}
$$

We put both terms over a common denominator, and combine the two fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}x}{\operatorname{sin}x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x} & =\frac{(1+\operatorname{cos}x)\operatorname{cos}x}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{sin}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x}+\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x}{\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{sin}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{cos}x+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}x+({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}x+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}x)}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}x+1}{\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that:

$$
\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $\mathbf{a}=⟨1,-3,2⟩,$ $\mathbf{b}=⟨2,-1,-1⟩,$ and $\mathbf{c}=⟨3,-3,0⟩,$ find $\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})$ using the definition of the scalar triple product.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the cross product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -3 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 3 & 0\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 3 & -3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((-1)\cdot 0-(-1)\cdot (-3))\mathbf{i}-(2\cdot 0-(-1)\cdot 3)\mathbf{j}+(2\cdot (-3)-(-1)\cdot 3)\mathbf{k} \\  & =-3\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-3,-3,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the scalar triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =⟨1,-3,2⟩\cdot ⟨-3,-3,-3⟩ \\  & =1\cdot (-3)+(-3)\cdot (-3)+2\cdot (-3) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $\mathbf{a}=⟨-2,4,3⟩,$ $\mathbf{b}=⟨-1,3,2⟩,$ and $\mathbf{c}=⟨2,-1,4⟩,$ find $\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})$ using the definition of the scalar triple product.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the cross product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 4\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(3\cdot 4-2\cdot (-1))\mathbf{i}-((-1)\cdot 4-2\cdot 2)\mathbf{j}+((-1)\cdot (-1)-3\cdot 2)\mathbf{k} \\  & =14\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j}-5\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨14,8,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the scalar triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =⟨-2,4,3⟩\cdot ⟨14,8,-5⟩ \\  & =(-2)\cdot 14+4\cdot 8+3\cdot (-5) \\  & =-11.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $\mathbf{a}=⟨-2,0,-1⟩,$ $\mathbf{b}=⟨-2,-1,0⟩,$ and $\mathbf{c}=⟨3,1,4⟩,$ find $\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c})$ using the definition of the scalar triple product.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the cross product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =((-1)\cdot 4-0\cdot 1)\mathbf{i}-((-2)\cdot 4-0\cdot 3)\mathbf{j}+((-2)\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot 3)\mathbf{k} \\  & =-4\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-4,8,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the scalar triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =⟨-2,0,-1⟩\cdot ⟨-4,8,1⟩ \\  & =(-2)\cdot (-4)+0\cdot 8+(-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{p}=⟨3,-2,1⟩$, $\mathbf{q}=⟨2,-1,0⟩$ and $\mathbf{r}=⟨1,-2,4⟩.$ Find $\mathbf{q}\cdot (\mathbf{r}\times \mathbf{p}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the scalar triple product $\mathbf{q}\cdot (\mathbf{r}\times \mathbf{p})$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $\mathbf{q},$ $\mathbf{r},$ and $\mathbf{p}.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{q}\cdot (\mathbf{r}\times \mathbf{p}) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-2 & 4 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix}-(-1)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}+0\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 3 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2((-2)\cdot 1-4\cdot (-2))+(1\cdot 1-4\cdot 3) \\  & =12-11 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{p}=⟨3,1,2⟩$, $\mathbf{q}=⟨1,-2,1⟩$ and $\mathbf{r}=⟨4,1,-2⟩.$ Find $\mathbf{r}\cdot (\mathbf{q}\times \mathbf{p}).$

Remember that the scalar triple product $\mathbf{r}\cdot (\mathbf{q}\times \mathbf{p})$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $\mathbf{r},$ $\mathbf{q},$ and $\mathbf{p}.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}\cdot (\mathbf{q}\times \mathbf{p}) & =\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}-1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{vmatrix}+(-2)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4((-2)\cdot 2-1\cdot 1)-(1\cdot 2-1\cdot 3)-2(1\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot 3) \\  & =-20+1-14 \\  & =-33.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $\mathbf{c}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{a})$, if $\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}=⟨3,-1,2⟩$ and $\mathbf{a}=⟨4,-2,6⟩.$

$$

Then, we swap $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ to get

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x=\sqrt{t-2}+1,\,\,\,y={t}^{3}+2,\,t\ge 2,
$$

what are the ranges of $x$ and $y?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ note that $\sqrt{t-2}\ge 0$ for all $t\ge 2.$ Consequently, $x=\sqrt{t-2}+1\ge 1.$

- To find the range of $y,$ note that ${t}^{3}\ge 8$ for all $t\ge 2.$ Consequently, $y={t}^{3}+2\ge 8+2=10.$

Therefore, the ranges are $x\ge 1$ and $y\ge 10.$

question.:question/problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x=1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,
$$

what are the ranges of $x$ and $y?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ notice that for $0\le \theta <2\pi ,$ we have $-1\le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{cos}\theta \le 1 \\ 2 & \text{ }{\color{red}\ge }-2\operatorname{cos}\theta \text{ }{\color{red}\ge }-2 \\ -2 & \le -2\operatorname{cos}\theta \le 2 \\ 1-2 & \le 1-2\operatorname{cos}\theta \le 1+2 \\ -1 & \le x\le 3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $-1\le x\le 3.$

- To find the range of $y,$ notice that for $0\le \theta <2\pi ,$ we have $-1\le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ -2 & \le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 2 \\ -2-3 & \le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -3\le 2-3 \\ -5 & \le y\le -1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $-5\le y\le -1.$

Therefore, the ranges are $-1\le x\le 3$ and $-5\le y\le -1.$

question.:question/problem:
Given that a curve is defined parametrically as

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1,\,\,\,y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{3}{2},\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,
$$

what are the ranges of $x$ and $y?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's consider each variable in turn.

- To find the range of $x,$ notice that for $0\le \theta <2\pi ,$ we have $-1\le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ -2 & \le 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \le 2 \\ -2+1 & \le 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1\le 2+1 \\ -1 & \le x\le 3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $-1\le x\le 3.$

- To find the range of $y,$ notice that for $0\le \theta <2\pi ,$ we have $-1\le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1.$ Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \le \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \le \frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2} & \le \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{3}{2}\le \frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & \le y\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can conclude that $1\le y\le 2.$

Therefore, the ranges are $-1\le x\le 3$ and $1\le y\le 2.$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}y{e}^{x}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the section of the curve $y=5x+2$ for $\,0\le x\le 1?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=5t+2.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,5t+2⟩,\hspace{2em}0\le t\le 1
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t+2)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+5\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{26}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=y{e}^{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =(5t+2){e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(5t+2){e}^{t}\cdot \sqrt{26}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{26}{\int }_{0}^{1}(5t+2){e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4},$ $\,0\le x\le 4\sqrt{6}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}⟩,\hspace{2em}0\le t\le 4\sqrt{6}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}\right)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+\frac{t}{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}\right)}{t}=\frac{t}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}\frac{t}{4}\cdot \sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}t\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}$, $\text{d}u=\frac{t}{2}\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4\sqrt{6}}t\sqrt{1+\frac{{t}^{2}}{4}}\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{25}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{3}{|}_{1}^{25} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({25}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(125-1) \\  & =\frac{124}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\frac{4{y}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{1}{x},$ $\,1\le x\le \sqrt[4]{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=\frac{1}{t}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{1}{t}⟩,\hspace{2em}1\le t\le \sqrt[4]{2}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(u) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{\left(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{4{y}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{4{\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)}^{2}}{{t}^{3}}=\frac{4}{{t}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}3{x}^{5}{y}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[4]{2}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[4]{2}}\frac{4}{{t}^{5}}\cdot \sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[4]{2}}\frac{1}{{t}^{5}}\hspace{0.167em}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}$, $\text{d}u=-\frac{4}{{t}^{5}}\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[4]{2}}\frac{1}{{t}^{5}}\,\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}}\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{3/2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{2}^{3/2} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}(\sqrt{{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}^{3}}-\sqrt{{2}^{3}}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}(\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{4}-2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(8\sqrt{2}-3\sqrt{6})\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}4,\hspace{0.222em}{t}^{2}⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2t⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+0+{(2t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\hspace{0.167em}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t\ge 0$ for $t\in [0,2].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2\sqrt{2}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}({t}^{2}){|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}{t}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=3.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}2t,\hspace{0.222em}2{t}^{2}⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(2t)}^{2}+{(2{t}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(1+2{t}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =1+2{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{3}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(1+2{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={(t+\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3})|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =3+18-0 \\  & =21.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $$

$$
from  $t=0$ to $t=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t\operatorname{cos}2t-\operatorname{sin}2t),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}\right),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t\operatorname{sin}2t+\operatorname{cos}2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-4t\operatorname{sin}2t,\hspace{0.222em}3t,\hspace{0.222em}4t\operatorname{cos}2t⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-4t\operatorname{sin}2t)}^{2}+(3t)^{2}+{(4t\operatorname{cos}2t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}2t+9{t}^{2}+16{t}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}2t} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}+9{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{t}^{2}} \\  & =5t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t\ge 0$ for $t\in [0,2].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\left(\frac{5{t}^{2}}{2}\right)|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf{g}(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2},\hspace{0.222em}2t⟩$ from $t=1$ to $t=e.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t}-t,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{t}-t)}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}-2+{t}^{2}+4} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}+2+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{t}+t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{t}+t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{e}‖{\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{1}{t}+t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}t+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}){|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}e+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2})-(\operatorname{ln}1+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =1+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-0-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}+1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
