Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t\operatorname{sin}t+\operatorname{cos}t,\hspace{0.222em}t\operatorname{cos}t-\operatorname{sin}t⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}t+\operatorname{cos}t),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}t-\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.222em}⟩ \\  & =⟨t\operatorname{cos}t,\hspace{0.222em}-t\operatorname{sin}t⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(t\operatorname{cos}t)}^{2}+{(-t\operatorname{sin}t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{t}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}} \\  & =t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t\ge 0$ for $t\in [0,2].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\right)|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

from  $t=1$ to $t=2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}2t+2t\operatorname{sin}2t),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}2t-2t\operatorname{cos}2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4t\operatorname{cos}2t\hspace{0.222em},4t\operatorname{sin}2t⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(4t\operatorname{cos}2t)}^{2}+{(4t\operatorname{sin}2t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+16{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}} \\  & =4t\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨2,x,1⟩,$ $\mathbf{b}=⟨1,-x,3⟩$ and $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|=10.$ Find $x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & x & 1 \\ 1 & -x & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}x & 1 \\ -x & 3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}2 & x \\ 1 & -x\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(3x+x)\mathbf{i}-(6-1)\mathbf{j}+(-2x-x)\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨4x,-5,-3x⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{(4x)^{2}+(-5)^{2}+(-3x)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+25+9{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25({x}^{2}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we solve for $x$ the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =10 \\ \sqrt{25({x}^{2}+1)} & =10 \\ 25({x}^{2}+1) & =100 \\ {x}^{2}+1 & =4 \\ {x}^{2} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\pm \sqrt{3}.$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨2,0,-4⟩,$ $\mathbf{b}=⟨-1,1,2x⟩$ and $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|=2\sqrt{5}.$ Find $x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 0 & -4 \\ -1 & 1 & 2x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & -4 \\ 1 & 2x\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}2 & -4 \\ -1 & 2x\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(0+4)\mathbf{i}-(4x-4)\mathbf{j}+(2-0)\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨4,-4x+4,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-4x+4)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+16{x}^{2}-32x+16+4} \\  & =\sqrt{16{x}^{2}-32x+36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we solve for $x$ the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{16{x}^{2}-32x+36} & =2\sqrt{5} \\ 16{x}^{2}-32x+36 & =20 \\ 16{x}^{2}-32x+16 & =0 \\ 16({x}^{2}-2x+1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+1 & =0 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =0 \\ x-1 & =0 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=1.$

question.:question/problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(1,6)?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$

question.:question/problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =7\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =49{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +49{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  \\  & =49({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta ) \\  & =49(1) \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=49.$

question.:question/problem:
Determine the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+1}{2} & =\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta  \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-4}{2} & =\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ \frac{(y-4)^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  \\ \frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4} & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4} & ={\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ (x+1)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $(x+1)^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{4} & =\operatorname{sin}\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta .\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $(x-5)^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$

question.:question/problem:
Which of the following vector fields are conservative on ${R}^{2}?$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

Note that for each of our functions, $D={R}^{2}.$ With this in mind, let's check each of the vector fields.

- For the vector field $F,$ we have $P=2xy$ and $Q={x}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $F$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $G,$ we have $P=\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})$ and $Q=2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}).$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}),\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $G$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $H,$ we have $P=y{e}^{xy}$ and $Q=x{e}^{xy}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $H$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is $F(x,y)=2xy\,i+{x}^{2}\,j$; $G(x,y)$ $=\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})\,i$ $+2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})\,j$; $H(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}\,i+x{e}^{xy}\,j$.

question.:question/problem:
If $D=\{(x,y)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}{x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}\le 4,\hspace{0.222em}x\ge 0\},$ then $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](images/96/968419bad65410864c75e8abe766d21ac4d4acd835c73ea84118cf21ac066f79.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=4$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =4 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta -2)^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta -4r\operatorname{sin}\theta +4 & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )-4r\operatorname{sin}\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-4r\operatorname{sin}\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-4\operatorname{sin}\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](images/2f/2fe33fb6e1be8b6107cb667e9453613af906bd4da7d67f9d9323d49cce5ae06c.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =0$ (the positive $x$-axis) and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the positive $y$-axis):

![](images/e2/e2b5e7b4433cbfb50ac7a9f991e4e4bc0cf8deecfefeeef0a4c9606ab6183cce.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta )\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le r\le 4\operatorname{sin}\theta ,\hspace{0.222em}0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta $ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({3}^{4}-{1}^{4})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =20{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate with respect to $\theta :$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}20{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  & =20[\frac{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }{2}]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =10{[{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =10({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}(0)) \\  & =10(1-0) \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ in the fourth quadrant is enclosed between two quarter-circles centered at $O$ of radii $1$ and $2,$ as shown above. What is
$$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A
$$
expressed in polar coordinates?
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

The region $D$ represents a portion of the washer enclosed between the circles of radii $1$ and $2$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta )\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}1\le r\le 2,\hspace{0.222em}-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}((r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2})\hspace{0.167em}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{3}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/ce/ce35f6ef14576f536c268dd7420af6e0226609ab5305e85770f400439c2435de.png)

Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,
$$ where the region $D$ is shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at $(\frac{1}{2},0)\,.$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $$
\displaystyle {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4},
$$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}\theta -\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta -r\operatorname{cos}\theta +\frac{1}{4}+{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )-r\operatorname{cos}\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-r\operatorname{cos}\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-\operatorname{cos}\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

- For $x=\frac{1}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$  So, the entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/f5/f518a206638071a7b8548882a453123b6d78aed0aa94cc0e6e23429f22c6f1b3.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta )\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}\theta \le r\le \operatorname{cos}\theta ,\hspace{0.222em}0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}\theta }{{r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{\operatorname{sec}\theta /2}^{\operatorname{cos}\theta }2\operatorname{cos}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}\theta {\int }_{\operatorname{sec}\theta /2}^{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}\theta [r]_{\operatorname{sec}\theta /2}^{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2\operatorname{cos}\theta (\operatorname{cos}\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(2{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta -1)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}(2\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{sin}(2\theta )]_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}{\int }_{2}^{4}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta =
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta $ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}{\int }_{2}^{4}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{2}^{4}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ({4}^{2}-{2}^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6{\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate with respect to $\theta :$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\int }_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =6[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{\pi /6}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =6(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{3\pi }{4}\right)-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right)) \\  & =6(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =3(\sqrt{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate 
$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{1}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta $ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1-\operatorname{cos}\theta }^{1}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\hspace{0.222em}[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]_{1-\operatorname{cos}\theta }^{1}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}({1}^{2}-(1-\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}\theta -{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate with respect to $\theta :$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}\theta -{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  & ={[\operatorname{sin}\theta -\frac{1}{4}\theta -\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}(2\theta )]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}\pi )-0 \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{8}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{8-\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Integrate the function $f(x,y)=\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ over the portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at the origin, where $x\le 0$ and $y\le 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](images/e4/e4275e74a45deb22c0ed22546772e33fbd5caeb89a4036b1a2f4870e8ecf67a1.png)

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2}{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{{r}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}[\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}+1)]_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2[\theta ]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2(\frac{3\pi }{2}-\pi ) \\  & =\frac{\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/d0/d0d72be437a462f5eea781e83cc2a95e956e11ddc3295ad3b02a4a57867d9271.png)

Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,
$$ where the region $D$ is shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin.

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ we obtain $r=2.$

- For $y=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-1 \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-1 \\ r & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(\sqrt{3},-1).$ So, the entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{6},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/23/2386c1dcb1cf71231f2bb508dc1dd85dadef15b806eaf7f9a9ad0d3e4f3da1ca.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,-\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{6}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}\theta }{{r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}{\int }_{-\operatorname{csc}\theta }^{2}2\operatorname{sin}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}2\operatorname{sin}\theta {\int }_{-\operatorname{csc}\theta }^{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}2\operatorname{sin}\theta [r]_{-\operatorname{csc}\theta }^{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}2\operatorname{sin}\theta (2+\operatorname{csc}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6}(4\operatorname{sin}\theta +2)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[-4\operatorname{cos}\theta +2\theta ]_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /6} \\  & =[(-4\operatorname{cos}\left(-\frac{\pi }{6}\right)-\frac{\pi }{3})-(0-\pi )] \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}-2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .

question.:question/problem:
![](images/15/15e58073c87bd249473950680a49e8fc4cb4be94277a7001c0ab9f96ab3a46df.png)

The region $D$ is enclosed between the curve $(x+2)^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ and the line $x=-3,$ as shown above. What is
$$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A
$$
expressed in polar coordinates?
question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(-2,0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $(x+2)^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}\theta +2)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +4r\operatorname{cos}\theta +4+{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )+4r\operatorname{cos}\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}+4r\operatorname{cos}\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+4\operatorname{cos}\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

- For $x=-3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-3 \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =-3 \\ r & =-\frac{3}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =-3\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the points $(-3,-\sqrt{3})$ and $(-3,\sqrt{3}).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{6}$ and $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{6},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/92/928c6dc79f44a2185ccf217c0cf9210630b6554a698f805ef2c77500f9ddc76b.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,-3\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \le r\le -4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{5\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{7\pi }{6}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{5\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}{\int }_{-3\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{5\pi /6}^{7\pi /6}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{-3\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:

- For $x=3,$ we get

$$

$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ we obtain $r=4.$

- For $x=2\sqrt{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\sqrt{2} \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =2\sqrt{2} \\ r & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(2\sqrt{2},2\sqrt{2}).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4},$ as depicted below.

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$

$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{6x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}\frac{6r\operatorname{cos}\theta }{{r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}\theta }^{4}6\operatorname{cos}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}6\operatorname{cos}\theta {\int }_{2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}\theta }^{4}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}6\operatorname{cos}\theta [r]_{2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}\theta }^{4}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}6\operatorname{cos}\theta (4-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(24\operatorname{cos}\theta -12\sqrt{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[24\operatorname{sin}\theta -12\sqrt{2}\hspace{0.167em}\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =[(24\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-12\sqrt{2}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))-0] \\  & =12\sqrt{2}-3\pi \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

Evaluate the double integral $$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(0,1).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-1)^{2} & =1 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta -1)^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta -2r\operatorname{sin}\theta +1 & =1 \\ {r}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )-2r\operatorname{sin}\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{sin}\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{sin}\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

- For $y=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =1 \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ r & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(-1,1).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/1b/1b83e2674bba4bd6c326083f8c94496b5288de23575dc63a92b9a660eba69f67.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \le r\le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{4}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{4y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A & ={∬}_{\mathrm{Δ}}\frac{4r\operatorname{sin}\theta }{{r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta }\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}{\int }_{\operatorname{csc}\theta }^{2\operatorname{sin}\theta }4\operatorname{sin}\theta \hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}4\operatorname{sin}\theta {\int }_{\operatorname{csc}\theta }^{2\operatorname{sin}\theta }\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}4\operatorname{sin}\theta [r]_{\operatorname{csc}\theta }^{2\operatorname{sin}\theta }\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}4\operatorname{sin}\theta (2\operatorname{sin}\theta -\operatorname{csc}\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta -1)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}(2\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-2[\operatorname{sin}(2\theta )]_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =-2[\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{sin}(\pi )] \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y},$ where $x={e}^{st}$ and $y={e}^{-st}.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{({e}^{st})^{2}}=-{e}^{-2st}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{1}{({e}^{-st})^{2}}=-{e}^{2st}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t{e}^{st}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =-t{e}^{-st}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(-{e}^{-2st})(t{e}^{st})+(-{e}^{2st})(-t{e}^{-st}) \\  & =t{e}^{st}-t{e}^{-st} \\  & =t({e}^{st}-{e}^{-st}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=xy,$ where $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(st)$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(st).$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂t}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(st), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(st).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =s\operatorname{cos}⁡(st), \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-s\operatorname{sin}⁡(st).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}(st))(s\operatorname{cos}(st))+(\operatorname{sin}(st))(-s\operatorname{sin}(st)) \\  & =s{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(st)-s{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}(st) \\  & =s({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}(st)-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}(st)) \\  & =s\operatorname{cos}(2st).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=3x-2y+z,$ where $x=s+t,$ $y={s}^{2}-{t}^{2}$ and $z=s.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂t}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/b5/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =-2t, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(3)\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot (-2t)+(1)\cdot 0 \\  & =4t+3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=xyz,$ where $x=2,$ $y=s{e}^{t}$ and $z=t{e}^{s}.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂t}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/b5/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=xz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =ts{e}^{t+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2t{e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2s{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =0, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =s{e}^{t}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =(ts{e}^{t+s})\cdot 0+(2t{e}^{s})\cdot s{e}^{t}+(2s{e}^{t})\cdot {e}^{s} \\  & =2ts{e}^{t+s}+2s{e}^{t+s} \\  & =2s(t+1){e}^{t+s}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x+y+z},$ where $x=s-t,$ $y={t}^{2}$ and $z=s+t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂t}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/b5/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+y+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x+y+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={e}^{x+y+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2},$ where $x=t+2s,$ $y=3t-s$ and $z=st.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(t+2s)=2t+4s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2(3t-s)=6t-2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(2t+4s)\cdot 2+(6t-2s)\cdot (-1)+(2st)\cdot t \\  & =4t+8s-6t+2s+2s{t}^{2} \\  & =10s-2t+2s{t}^{2} \\  & =2(5s-t+s{t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2{e}^{y}+4z,$ where $x=t{s}^{2},$ $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+{s}^{2})$ and $z={s}^{2}.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$

![](images/be/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{t{s}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+{s}^{2})}=-2({t}^{2}+{s}^{2}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2ts, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\frac{2s}{{t}^{2}+{s}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\left(\frac{1}{t{s}^{2}}\right)\cdot 2ts+(-2({t}^{2}+{s}^{2}))\cdot \left(\frac{2s}{{t}^{2}+{s}^{2}}\right)+(4)\cdot 2s \\  & =\frac{2}{s}-4s+8s \\  & =\frac{2}{s}+4s \\  & =\frac{2(1+2{s}^{2})}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{e}^{y},x=2t$ and $y={t}^{2},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}.$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2t){e}^{{t}^{2}}=4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2t)^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}=4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2xy},x=t$ and $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡t,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}.$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{2xy}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{2xy}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}\cdot 1+\frac{t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}} \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{ln}⁡t}{\sqrt{2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1.\end{aligned}

$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y},x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2s$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}2s}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}2s}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}2s)+\left(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}2s}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}2s}\right)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}2s \\  & =-2-2\cdot \frac{{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}2s}{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}2s} \\  & =-2-2{\operatorname{cot}}^{2}2s \\  & =-2{\operatorname{csc}}^{2}2s.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{1+y},$ $x={s}^{2}$ and $y=s,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{1+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{(1+y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{1+s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+s}\cdot 2s-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{2s}{1+s}-\frac{{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2s(1+s)-{s}^{2}}{(1+s)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{s(2+s)}{(1+s)^{2}}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{x+y}$ and $y={e}^{-x},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$

$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and $y={x}^{3},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{x}^{6}}} \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}(1+{x}^{4})}} \\  & =\frac{x}{x\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{x}^{6}}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}(1+{x}^{4})}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{x\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+yx$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y)$ and $y=\frac{1}{x},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}))\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\right) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\left(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}}\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x}\right).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x+1}$ and $y={x}^{3},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=(3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}\pi y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(ax-\pi x\operatorname{sin}\pi y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ where $a$ is a constant. Given that $\mathbf{F}$ is conservative, find the value of $a.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=P(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ be a vector field with domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$\mathbf{F}$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

For the vector field $\mathbf{F},$ the domain $D={\mathbb{R}}^{2},$ and we have 

$$
P=3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y,\,Q=ax-\pi x\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi y.
$$

Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=a-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi y.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi y & =a-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi y \\ a & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a=0.$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+Q\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

* the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf{r}(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

* the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf{T}(t).$

Parameterizing the line segment $L,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{2}t,\,y=-\sqrt{2}t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the line from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(\sqrt{2},-\sqrt{2}).$ Therefore, $\mathbf{n}$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf{T},$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x{y}^{2} \\  & =3(\sqrt{2}t)(-\sqrt{2}t)^{2} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}{t}^{3}, \\ Q(x,y) & =-{y}^{3} \\  & =-(-\sqrt{2}t)^{3} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}t)=\sqrt{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\sqrt{2}t)=-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{L}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathbf{n}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{L}P\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y-Q\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6\sqrt{2}{t}^{3})\cdot (-\sqrt{2})-(2\sqrt{2}{t}^{3})\cdot (\sqrt{2})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-12{t}^{3}-4{t}^{3})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-16{t}^{3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =-4[{t}^{4}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-4(1-0) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

As we saw earlier, we can use Green's theorem to write our line integral in polar coordinates as 

$$
{∮}_{∂R}3x{y}^{2}\,dx-{y}^{3}\,dy={∬}_{Δ}-3{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta .

\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta )\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}1\le r\le 2,\hspace{0.222em}0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{Δ}-3{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-3{[\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-2}]}_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{r=1}^{r=2}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(1-1)\cdot \frac{1}{4}({2}^{4}-{1}^{4}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨5,\sqrt{2},0⟩$ and $\mathbf{b}=⟨-1,1,0⟩.$ Find $\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}.$

question.:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}=⟨4,2,-1⟩$, $\mathbf{b}=⟨x,2,-1⟩$ and $|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}|=\sqrt{20}.$ Find $x.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 4 & 2 & -1 \\ x & 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}-\begin{vmatrix}4 & -1 \\ x & -1\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j}+\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 \\ x & 2\end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(-2+2)\mathbf{i}-(-4+x)\mathbf{j}+(8-2x)\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨0,4-x,8-2x⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(4-x)^{2}+(8-2x)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16-8x+{x}^{2}+64-32x+4{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-40x+80}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we solve for $x$ the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{a}\times \mathbf{b}\hspace{0.167em}| & =\sqrt{20} \\ \sqrt{5{x}^{2}-40x+80} & =\sqrt{20} \\ 5{x}^{2}-40x+80 & =20 \\ 5{x}^{2}-40x+60 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-8x+12 & =0 \\ (x-2)(x-6) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=2,\,6.$

question.:question/problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=1.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates.

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/f4/f4c6f3acefa5d89fd5064de469952da3d68d379559bb4a6a4990a2ea24e4f861.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $1$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=1.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta ,z)\hspace{0.167em}:\hspace{0.167em}0\le r\le 1,\hspace{0.222em}0\le \theta <2\pi ,\hspace{0.222em}0\le z\le 1\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{z}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V & ={∭}_{\mathrm{Δ}}{z}^{2}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2}}\cdot r\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}z\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{\mathrm{Δ}}r{z}^{2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )}\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}z\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{{\color{blue}1}}}{\int }_{0}^{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{{\color{blue}1}}}\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{{\color{blue}{r}^{2}{z}^{2}}}\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}z\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V & ={∭}_{\mathrm{Δ}}\frac{z}{\sqrt{{r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}\theta }}\hspace{0.222em}r\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}z\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}(2\theta )}}z\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}z\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}(2\theta )}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}{(\sqrt{9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}(2\theta )})}^{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{2}(9-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}(2\theta ))\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{9}{2}r-\frac{1}{6}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}(2\theta )]}_{r=0}^{r=3}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{9}{2}(3)-\frac{1}{6}(3)^{3}\operatorname{cos}(2\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{27}{2}-\frac{9}{2}\operatorname{cos}(2\theta )\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[\frac{27}{2}\theta -\frac{9}{4}\operatorname{sin}(2\theta )]}_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi } \\  & =\frac{27}{2}(2\pi -0)-\frac{9}{4}(0-0) \\  & =27\pi .\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
If the solid region $R$ is given by 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}:\hspace{0.167em}(x-3)^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9,\hspace{0.222em}y\le 0,\hspace{0.222em}y\le z\le 6\},
$$

then $$
\displaystyle {∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z+1}}\,\text{d}V=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/cc/ccc5cab37aed89c0d701ce0195414796211ddc73a498eaaa1ff145a45c42e9fd.png)

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis passes through the point $(3,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and

- bounded above by $z=6.$

With that in mind, let's now write the $(x-3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =9 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}\theta -3)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2} & =3 \\ {r}^{2}{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta -6r\operatorname{cos}\theta +9+{r}^{2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta  & =9 \\ {r}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )-6r\operatorname{cos}\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-6r\operatorname{cos}\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-6\operatorname{cos}\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta ,z)\hspace{0.167em}:\hspace{0.167em}0\le r\le 6\operatorname{cos}\theta ,\hspace{0.222em}\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\hspace{0.222em}r\operatorname{sin}\theta \le z\le 6\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z+1}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V & ={∭}_{\mathrm{Δ}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z+1}}\cdot r\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}z\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{{\color{blue}6\operatorname{cos}\theta }}}{\int }_{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{{\color{blue}r\operatorname{sin}\theta }}}^{6}\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{{\color{blue}\frac{r}{\sqrt{z+1}}}}\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}z\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y
$$

represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the functions $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)?$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
According to Green's theorem, if 

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Pair “$P(x,y)={e}^{x+y}-\frac{y}{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{x+y}+\frac{x}{2}$” gives the required area.  In this case,
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{x+y}-\frac{1}{2}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{x+y}+\frac{1}{2},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

- Pair “$P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$” does *not* give the required area.  Notice that 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡y$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y\ne 1.
$$

- Pair “$P(x,y)=x$ and $Q(x,y)=x$” gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is “$P(x,y)={e}^{x+y}-\frac{y}{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{x+y}+\frac{x}{2}$”; “$P(x,y)=x$ and $Q(x,y)=x$” only.

question.:question/problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$

represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the vector field $F(x,y)?$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
According to Green's theorem, if $F(x,y)=⟨P(x,y),\,Q(x,y)⟩,$ where

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Vector field $F(x,y)=⟨0,\,x⟩$ give the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

- Pair $F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{y},\,y⟩$ does *not* give the required area. In this case, 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{y}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{e}^{y}\ne 1.
$$

- Pair $$
\displaystyle F(x,y)=⟨-\frac{y}{5}+\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,\,\frac{4x}{5}⟩
$$ gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{5}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{4}{5},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $F(x,y)=⟨0,\,x⟩$; $$
\displaystyle F(x,y)=⟨-\frac{y}{5}+\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,\,\frac{4x}{5}⟩
$$ only.

question.:question/problem:

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region enclosed by the curve 
$C$ parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t)=2\operatorname{sin}2t\hspace{0.222em}\mathbf{i}-2\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.222em}\mathbf{j}$ 
for $t\in [0,\pi ].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented. 

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =4\operatorname{cos}2t\hspace{0.222em}\mathbf{i}-2\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.222em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}x\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}2t\cdot (-2\operatorname{cos}t)\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}2t\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t\cdot \operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}t{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =-8{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & =8{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=-{x}^{4}y-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=x{y}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{4}-{x}^{2}{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{4}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}-({x}^{4}y+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3})\,dx+(x{y}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{4}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-(-{x}^{4}-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+{y}^{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta )\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}1\le r\le 3,\hspace{0.222em}0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}((r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2})^{2}\cdot r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{4}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )^{2}\cdot r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{5}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta {\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{5}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{5}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi \cdot {\frac{1}{6}{r}^{6}|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot ({3}^{6}-{1}^{6}) \\  & =\frac{728\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

{∮}_{∂D}(\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x+(\operatorname{ln}({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}y)-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y,
$$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}y)-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}={y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-{x}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}(\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x+(\operatorname{ln}({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}y)-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$
\mathrm{Δ}=\{(r,\theta )\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}2\le r\le 4,\hspace{0.222em}0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{4}-((r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2})\cdot r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{4}-{r}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}\theta +{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}\theta )\cdot r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{2}^{4}-{r}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}\theta {\int }_{2}^{4}-{r}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r \\  & =-2\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}{r}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}r \\  & =-2\pi \cdot {\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot ({4}^{4}-{2}^{4}) \\  & =-120\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/b2/b232a4cddf05a425709c1b3204b69b0126e586b42a6af73b867dd75ee294d961.png)

Calculate 
$$
\displaystyle {∮}_{∂D}({x}^{3}{y}^{3}+x)\,dx+({x}^{4}{y}^{2}-y)\,dy,
$$
where $D$ is the region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{3}+x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{4}{y}^{2}-y.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3{x}^{3}{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4{x}^{3}{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}({x}^{3}{y}^{3}+x)\,dx+({x}^{4}{y}^{2}-y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-3{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as ${Δ}_{1}∖{Δ}_{2},$ where

- ${\mathrm{Δ}}_{1}=\{(x,y)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}-2\le x\le 2,-1\le y\le 2\}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- ${\mathrm{Δ}}_{2}=\{(x,y)\hspace{0.222em}:\hspace{0.222em}0\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 1\}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{Δ}_{1}}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{{Δ}_{2}}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\,{|}_{-2}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\,{|}_{-1}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\,{|}_{0}^{1}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(4-4)\cdot (\frac{8}{3}-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right))-(\frac{1}{4}-0)\cdot (\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =0\cdot 3-\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

Calculate 
$$
\displaystyle {∮}_{∂D}(x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})\,dx+(2{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3})\,dy,
$$
where $D$ is the region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4xy.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}(x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})\,dx+(2{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy-2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as ${Δ}_{1}∖{Δ}_{2},$ where

- ${Δ}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,-1\le y\le 2\}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- ${Δ}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 1\}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{Δ}_{1}}2xy\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{{Δ}_{2}}2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}2xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}2xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-1}^{2}y\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-1}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={x}^{2}\,{|}_{-2}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{2}-{x}^{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{1}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(4-4)\cdot (2-\frac{1}{2})-(1-1)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =0\cdot \frac{3}{2}-0\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}t,\hspace{0.222em}2\operatorname{sin}t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is

$$
{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.222em}2\operatorname{cos}t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3\operatorname{cos}t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{6{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t}\hspace{0.222em}\mathrm{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.167em}\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.167em}\operatorname{cos}t⟩$
from $t=0$ to $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t),\hspace{0.167em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t))⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.167em}\operatorname{cos}t,\hspace{0.167em}-\operatorname{sin}t⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}t\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}(1-0) \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
