question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+25{y}^{2}=100.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $5$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={e}^{y}={e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={e}^{x}={e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitutions $u=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,du=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt$ and $v=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,dv=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u+{\int }_{1}^{1}{e}^{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/62/62c8f6d7db345ce76bd164bb52c13e5edef9c04f18f4f07501c8694e7f64b554.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $x={e}^{y}$ from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{2}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={e}^{t}\,y=t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/ba/ba6285008fd90835fdbf73203b76a0a01d713889d9939979aaec54bebd0a8c49.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}={t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x}={e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2})\cdot (1)-({e}^{-t})\cdot ({e}^{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$

$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={e}^{y}={e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={e}^{x}={e}^{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitutions $u=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,du=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt$ and $v=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,dv=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({e}^{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}{e}^{u}\,du-{\int }_{1}^{1}{e}^{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+(x+y)\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =x+y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }15{cos}^{2}⁡t+9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+15{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }15\,\text{d}t+9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }15\,\text{d}t+9{\int }_{0}^{0}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =15t{|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =15(2\pi -0) \\  & =30\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/95/95e6a455863f0b4cefe184cca9ad86feaeff9f0702808db2d151f5d6615a04b8.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{1}{x}$ from the point $(\frac{1}{2},2)$ to the point $(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={x}^{2}y\,i-y\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=\frac{1}{t},\,t\in [\frac{1}{2},2].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(\frac{1}{2},2)$ to the point $(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/cc/cc9d66f800a57f27673577cd3fd179b4cd6ff64585c5dc1a867317d8d592e485.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y=t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-y=-\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(t)\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\right)-\left(-\frac{1}{t}\right)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,{y}^{2}-{z}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=-x-y$ for $-2\le x\le 2$ and $-2\le y\le 2.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,-u-v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,-2\le v\le 2\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,{y}^{2}-{z}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=-u-v} \\  & =⟨{u}^{2}-{v}^{2},\,{v}^{2}-(-u-v)^{2},\,(-u-v)^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨{u}^{2}-{v}^{2},\,{v}^{2}-(-u-v)^{2},\,(-u-v)^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\cdot (1)+({v}^{2}-(-u-v)^{2})\cdot (1)+(-u-v)^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & ={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}+{v}^{2}-(-u-v)^{2}+(-u-v)^{2} \\  & ={u}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,{y}^{2}-{z}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For a surface $S$ given by $z={x}^{2}y$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,xy+\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,{x}^{2}+R)\,\text{d}A.
$$

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $z={x}^{2}y,$ it can be parameterized as

$$
r(x,y)=⟨x,\,y,\,{x}^{2}y⟩.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,0,\,2xy⟩ \\ {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨0,\,1,\,{x}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2xy \\ 0 & 1 & {x}^{2}\end{vmatrix}=⟨-2xy,\,-{x}^{2},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,y))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩\cdot ⟨-2xy,\,-{x}^{2},\,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2P\,xy+(\,-Q\,)\,{x}^{2}+R)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨(x+y)^{2},\,(x-y)^{2},\,xy⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=y-x$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $-3\le y\le 0.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-3}^{0}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,v-u⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,-3\le v\le 0\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨(x+y)^{2},\,(x-y)^{2},\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=v-u} \\  & =⟨(u+v)^{2},\,(u-v)^{2},\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨(u+v)^{2},\,(u-v)^{2},\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u+v)^{2}\cdot 1+(u-v)^{2}\cdot (-1)+uv\cdot 1 \\  & =5uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨(x+y)^{2},\,(x-y)^{2},\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5uv)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-3}^{0}5uv\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+z,\,2z,\,y+z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x-3y$ for $-1\le x\le 2$ and $-1\le y\le 3.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{3}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u-3v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 2,\,-1\le v\le 3\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,3,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x+z,\,2z,\,y+z⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-3v} \\  & =⟨u+u-3v,\,2(u-3v),\,v+u-3v⟩ \\  & =⟨2u-3v,\,2u-6v,\,u-2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨2u-3v,\,2u-6v,\,u-2v⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,3,\,1⟩ \\  & =(2u-3v)\cdot (-1)+(2u-6v)\cdot (3)+(u-2v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-2u+3v+6u-18v+u-2v \\  & =5u-17v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z-y,\,2y-z,\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5u-17v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{3}(5u-17v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the scalar field $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{3}.$ Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $C$ is any smooth path from $(-4,1)$ to $(0,-2)$ in ${R}^{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

In our case, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path $C$ are $A(-4,1)$ and $B(0,-2).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(0,-2)-f(-4,1) \\  & =({0}^{2}-2(-2)^{3})-((-4)^{2}-2(1)^{3}) \\  & =16-16+2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $F=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j,$ what is $\text{div}\,F?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement $∇\cdot F>0$ is true, whereas statements $∇\cdot F=0$ and $∇\cdot F<0$ are false. Notice that the lengths of the vector's $y$-components increase as we move vertically away from the origin. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a source at every point.

- Statement “$F$ is solenoidal” is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is $∇\cdot F>0$ only.

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F={y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,i+x\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j.$ 
Evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(\pi ,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =2{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\frac{x}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(\pi ,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\cdot F)(\pi ,1) & =2(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )+\frac{\pi }{1} \\  & =2(1)(1)+\pi  \\  & =2+\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $F=(x+y)^{2}\,i+(y+z)^{2}\,j+(x+z)^{2}\,k.$ Evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(-2,1,-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+y)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((y+z)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}((x+z)^{2}) \\  & =2(x+y)+2(y+z)+2(x+z) \\  & =4(x+y+z).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(-2,1,-1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F(-2,1,-1) & =4((-2)+(1)+(-1)) \\  & =4\cdot (-2) \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/a5/a56bcec93b5cc66ef8238b7fe7b213c5e184f1cf4b11baf4524525a63a284780.png)

Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,
$$ where the region $D$ is enclosed between two circles centered at $O$ of radii $1$ and $3,$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents the annulus between the disks of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at the origin. 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ we obtain $r=1.$

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ we obtain $r=3.$

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(9-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{26}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{26}{3}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{26}{3}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{52\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

The region $D$ is enclosed between the curve ${x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=4$ and the line $y=3,$ as shown above. What is
$$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A
$$
expressed in polar coordinates?
question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=4,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =4 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2)^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4 & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

- For $y=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3 \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =3 \\ r & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =3\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(-\sqrt{3},3).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\theta =\frac{2\pi }{3},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/49/4903ca2ba8cde3f7874e10998a0741035ec7b2dea69a7804eaca64cb552fc572.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,3\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \le r\le 4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{2\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi /3}{\int }_{3\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\frac{{r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi /3}{\int }_{3\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi /3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{3\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{y}-4xy,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2xy⟩
$$

through the boundary of the rectangle $-1\le x\le 1,-1\le y\le 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/9e/9e0bf7b88eadd199edc1997410b7ddbaa74b204e7d0f8afef7c9b17c28d8f8dc.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{y}-4xy$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4y+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(2x-4y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[{x}^{2}-4yx]_{-1}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[({1}^{2}-4y(1))-((-1)^{2}-4y(-1))]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}-8y\,dy \\  & =-4{y}^{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(-4(-1)^{2}) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{3}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/e6/e6f6a5cf9b37fe16f17fe74face946d85b426badf8db710ca4a7ea308a1ff2ec.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=14xy$ and $Q(x,y)=6{x}^{2}y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=14y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =6{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{3}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(14y+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{3}}(14y+6{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7{y}^{2}+6{x}^{2}y)\,{|}_{0}^{{x}^{3}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(7{x}^{6}+6{x}^{5})\,dx \\  & =({x}^{7}+{x}^{6})\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=-y,$ $\,x=\sqrt{y},$ and the line $y=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/2e/2ecabe22395006f0c7ef0a3f914087fa324f4d59c7d7886c18907f824744643e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+y$ and $Q(x,y)=xy+1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y\le x\le \sqrt{y},\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y}^{\sqrt{y}}3x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{-y}^{\sqrt{y}}\,dy \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/01/014c2310bcac5b6e9c2be2107bf8a5613b689ff29a8018d2be74fc607dd996db.png)

Find the arc length of the curve $r(t)=⟨7-2{t}^{3},3{t}^{2}+10⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=\sqrt{3}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7-2{t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+10)⟩ \\  & =⟨-6{t}^{2},\,6t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-6{t}^{2})^{2}+(6t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{t}^{4}+36{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{t}^{2}({t}^{2}+1)} \\  & =6t\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t\ge 0$ for $t\in [0,\sqrt{3}].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}6t\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u={t}^{2}+1$, $\text{d}u=2t\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}3\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot 2t\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}3\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2(8-1) \\  & =14\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ for $x\le 0$ and $y\ge 0,$ between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\text{d}V
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/8d/8dc4ea0ad2bb776fb31132e1ff8d97efdd2c166dc23ffbc8641f8d7034b8d487.png)

The region $R$ is one-quarter of a right vertical cylinder of radius $1$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}=\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\text{d}V & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}r\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$

- bounded above by $z=4-x=4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,\,0\le z\le 4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}({(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2})\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}[z]_{z=0}^{z=4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}(4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}4{r}^{3}-{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[{r}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]}_{r=0}^{r=1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[\theta -\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi } \\  & =(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{5}(0-0) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}

First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta $ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2}2r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}[{r}^{2}]_{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}({2}^{2}-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}(4-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}(4-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  & =[4\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ]_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}+\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right))-(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+\operatorname{cot}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)) \\  & =(2\pi +0)-(\pi +1) \\  & =\pi -1\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Let $S$ be the boundary of the finite solid region enclosed by the planes $x=0,$ $x=1,$ $z=0,$ $z=1,$ and the surfaces $y={x}^{2}$ and $y=x-z+2.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F=z\,i-4y\,j+{z}^{3}\,k,$ the flux of $F$ across $S$ can be written as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS=
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{3}) \\  & =0-4+3{z}^{2} \\  & =3{z}^{2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}(3{z}^{2}-4)\,\text{d}V,
$$

where $R$ is a type III solid region that can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le x-z+2\}.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}(3{z}^{2}-4)\,\text{d}V & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x-z+2}\,3{z}^{2}-4\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=-1,$ $x=2,$ $y=0,$ $y=1,$ $z=-1,$ $z=2.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F=y{z}^{2}\,i-2yz\,j+3{z}^{2}\,k,$ find the flux of $F$ across $S.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{z}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2yz)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(3{z}^{2}) \\  & =0+(-2z)+6z \\  & =4z.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}4z\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2}4z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{-1}^{2}4z\,\text{d}z \\  & =(2-(-1))\cdot (1-0)\cdot [2{z}^{2}]_{z=-1}^{z=2} \\  & =3\cdot 1\cdot (8-2) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=0,$ $x=1,$ $y=1,$ $y=3,$ $z=0,$ $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡3.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F=(y+{z}^{2})\,i-x\,j+3{x}^{2}{e}^{z}\,k,$ find the flux of $F$ across $S.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y+{z}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-x)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(3{x}^{2}{e}^{z}) \\  & =0+0+3{x}^{2}{e}^{z} \\  & =3{x}^{2}{e}^{z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}3{x}^{2}{e}^{z}\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}3{x}^{2}{e}^{z}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{1}^{3}\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =[{x}^{3}]_{x=0}^{x=1}\cdot (3-1)\cdot [{e}^{z}]_{z=0}^{z=\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =({1}^{3}-{0}^{3})\cdot 2\cdot ({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =1\cdot 2\cdot (3-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the positively (outward) oriented surface $S$ given by ${x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}+{z}^{2}=9$ and the vector field $F=(yz-2x)\,i+3y\,j+(x+z)\,k.$ Use the divergence theorem to find the flux of $F$ across $S.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz-2x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+z) \\  & =-2+3+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid sphere of radius $3$ enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}2\,\text{d}V \\  & =2{∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V \\  & =2\cdot \text{Volume}(R) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi \cdot {3}^{3} \\  & =72\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r
$$

represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the vector field $F(x,y)?$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
According to Green's theorem, if $F(x,y)=⟨P(x,y),\,Q(x,y)⟩,$ where

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Vector field $F(x,y)=⟨y{e}^{x},\,x-{e}^{x}⟩$ does *not* give the required area. In this case, 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{x}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1-{e}^{x},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-2{e}^{x}\ne 1.
$$

- Vector field $F(x,y)=⟨2y,\,x⟩$ does *not* give the required area. Notice that 
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1\ne 1.
$$

- Vector field $F(x,y)$ $$
\displaystyle =⟨-\frac{y}{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{2},\,\frac{2x}{3}+1⟩
$$ gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{3}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{2}{3},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $F(x,y)$ $$
\displaystyle =⟨-\frac{y}{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{2},\,\frac{2x}{3}+1⟩
$$ only.

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{5\pi }{3}].$ 
The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

*Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}-x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{5\pi /3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region enclosed by the curve 
$C$ parametrized as $r(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,j$ 
for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3\pi }{2}].$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,dx & =-{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2},$ where 

- ${C}_{1}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{1}(t)={t}^{5}\,i-2{t}^{4}\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1],$ and

- ${C}_{2}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{2}(t)=-t\,i-2\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ 

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and   

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{t}^{4}\,i-8{t}^{3}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-i\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}x\,dy-{∮}_{{C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{5}\cdot (-8{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{8}\,\text{d}t+0 \\  & =8[\frac{{t}^{9}}{9}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =8\cdot \frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{16}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose that $F$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ defined over the region $D$ above. Given that 

$$
{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=4,\,{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-6,\,{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-8,
$$

where ${C}_{1},$ ${C}_{2},$ and ${C}_{3}$ are oriented clockwise, calculate the value of $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the total circulation of a vector field over the boundary of a region containing holes, we add together the circulations over each *positively oriented* boundary.

Remember that:

- the positive direction is *counterclockwise* for the *outer* curve ${C}_{1}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{1}$ counterclockwise), and

- the positive direction is *clockwise* for the *inner* curves ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ (because the region $D$ is always on the left as we traverse ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ clockwise).

The diagram below shows the positive orientations of all three curves.

![](images/fa/fa1022d2a1718627898289abdd4d3035a6e06230eea16d0e46832675b2e37def.png)

Notice that the positive orientation of the outer curve ${C}_{1}$ is opposite that of ${C}_{1}$ as stated in the question.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}F\cdot \text{d}r & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{∮}_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-4+(-6)+(-8) \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/b1/b1a063fd261e790a8c3a56f741d0356f963300c3fbd88ddde03aa1744ef81053.png)

Calculate $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{∂D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,dx+({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{3})\,dy,
$$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{4}$ and $Q(x,y)=({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{3}).$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4{y}^{3},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,dx+({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}-(-4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3{x}^{2}y+3{y}^{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}3\cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot ((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}3{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}3{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{1}^{4}3{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\cdot \frac{3{r}^{5}}{5}\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))\cdot (\frac{3(4)^{5}}{5}-\frac{3(1)^{5}}{5}) \\  & =(1-1)\cdot (\frac{3(4)^{5}}{5}-\frac{3(1)^{5}}{5}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=-{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}-({x}^{2}y+{y}^{3})\,dx+({x}^{3}+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =8\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =8\pi \cdot {\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =2\pi \cdot ({3}^{4}-{1}^{4}) \\  & =160\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}{y}^{2}(x+1)\,dx+(3{x}^{2}y+2xy)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(6xy+2y)-2y(x+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- ${Δ}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 3,-1\le y\le 2\}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- ${Δ}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,0\le y\le 1\}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

$$

$$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A
$$
expressed in polar coordinates?
question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(0,0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ we obtain $r=2.$

- For $y=\sqrt{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{2} \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\sqrt{2} \\ r & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/89/897028515a29fdc4174d2a101439a81a30895db41ac3d29f311d53e0e6a79e29.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta \le r\le 2,\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.:question/problem: What is the equation of the level curve that passes through the point $P(3,-1)$ for the function $f(x,y)=\frac{2}{x-y}?$

First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,-1) & =\frac{2}{3-(-1)} \\  & =\frac{2}{3+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the level curve that passes through $P(3,-1)$ is the $\frac{1}{2}$-level curve.

Recall that the level curves for the function $f(x,y)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=\frac{1}{2}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =c \\ \frac{2}{x-y} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ 4 & =x-y \\ y & =x-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level curve that passes through $P(3,-1)$ is the line $y=x-4.$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/a1/a16e4559960b923535cadecb1e623592c07fa11de5929e722cffb85679195a66.png)

Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{3/4}\,\text{d}A,
$$ where the region $D$ is enclosed between two circles centered at $O$ of radii $1$ and $4,$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents the annulus between the disks of radii $1$ and $4$ centered at the origin. 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ we obtain $r=1.$

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ we obtain $r=4.$

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{3/4}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}{((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})}^{3/4}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}({r}^{2})^{3/4}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}{r}^{3/2}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}{r}^{5/2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{2}{7}{r}^{7/2}]}_{1}^{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{7}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(128-1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{254}{7}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{254}{7}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{254}{7}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{508\pi }{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Find $b\cdot (c\times a)$, if $b\times c=⟨2,-5,7⟩$ and $a=⟨8,-2,-4⟩.$

First, we compute the triple scalar product 

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =⟨8,-2,-4⟩\cdot ⟨2,-5,7⟩ \\  & =8\cdot 2+(-2)\cdot (-5)+(-4)\cdot 7 \\  & =16+10-28 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $a$ and $b$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}b\cdot (a\times c)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

and again we swap $a$ and $c$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}b\cdot (c\times a) & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

and again we swap $a$ and $b$ to get

question.:question/problem: Given that $a=⟨5,-8,-7⟩,$ $b=⟨-1,1,2⟩,$ and $c=⟨-3,1,0⟩,$ find $a\cdot (b\times c)$ using the definition of the scalar triple product.

First, we find the cross product:

$$
\begin{aligned}b\times c & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -3 & 0\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ -3 & 1\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =(1\cdot 0-1\cdot 2)i-(-1\cdot 0-(-3)\cdot 2)j+((-1)\cdot 1-(-3)\cdot 1)k \\  & =-2i-6j+2k \\  & =⟨-2,-6,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the scalar triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =⟨5,-8,-7⟩\cdot ⟨-2,-6,2⟩ \\  & =5\cdot (-2)+(-8)\cdot (-6)+(-7)\cdot 2 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting given vectors into the formula for the scalar triple product, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =⟨2\sqrt{2},\,-1,\,4⟩\cdot ⟨-2\sqrt{2},\,3,\,-5⟩ \\  & =(2\sqrt{2})(-2\sqrt{2})+(-1)(3)+(4)(-5) \\  & =-8-3-20 \\  & =-31.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we factor out the constants and get

$$
\begin{aligned}5a\cdot ((-4b)\times (-3c)) & =-120 \\ 5\cdot (-4)\cdot (-3)\cdot [a\cdot (b\times c)] & =-120 \\ 60[a\cdot (b\times c)] & =-120 \\ a\cdot (b\times c) & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $a$ and $b$ to get

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F=xyz\,i+{y}^{3}{x}^{2}\,j+y{z}^{2}\,k.$ 
Find $\text{div}\,F.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}{x}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(y{z}^{2}) \\  & =yz+3{y}^{2}{x}^{2}+2yz \\  & =3yz+3{y}^{2}{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2x})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y{e}^{2x})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(-z{e}^{2x}) \\  & =2{e}^{2x}-{e}^{2x}-{e}^{2x} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

$$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+(y+3)^{2}=9$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y+3)^{2} & =9 \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3)}^{2} & =9 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +6r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +9 & =9 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+6r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}+6r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region):

Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}2(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=x-y,$ where $x=-s\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=s\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂s}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/21/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =1, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+(-1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=(1-{y}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=(1-{y}^{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(1-{cos}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x={sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & ={sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/23/23d35daa15e11899592683f2f3215506cc0337358be843780dbf1190c0e38e2c.png)

Calculate $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{∂D}({x}^{2}+{e}^{x})\,dx+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{3/2}\,dy,
$$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+{e}^{x}$ and $Q(x,y)=({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{3/2}.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}({x}^{2}+{e}^{x})\,dx+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{3/2}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-0\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,4\le r\le 8,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{4}^{8}3\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{4}^{8}3\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{4}^{8}3{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{4}^{8}3{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{4}^{8}3{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\cdot \frac{3{r}^{4}}{4}\,{|}_{4}^{8} \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))\cdot (\frac{3(8)^{4}}{4}-\frac{3(4)^{4}}{4}) \\  & =0\cdot (\frac{3(8)^{4}}{4}-\frac{3(4)^{4}}{4}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
where $D$ is the region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=2x{y}^{3}+{x}^{5}$ and $Q(x,y)=5{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-{y}^{3}.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=6x{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=10x{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}(2x{y}^{3}+{x}^{5})\,dx+(5{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-{y}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}10x{y}^{2}-6x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as ${Δ}_{1}∖{Δ}_{2},$ where

- ${Δ}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 2,-2\le y\le 1\}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- ${Δ}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,-1\le y\le 0\}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{Δ}_{1}}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{{Δ}_{2}}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}4x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}4x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-2}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}4x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-1}^{0}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{x}^{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\,{|}_{-2}^{1}-2{x}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}\,{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =(8-2)\cdot (\frac{1}{3}-\left(-\frac{8}{3}\right))-(2-0)\cdot (0-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)) \\  & =6\cdot 3-2\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =18-\frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{52}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate $$

$$ where $D$ is the region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=4y$ and $Q(x,y)=5x.$ So, 

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=5.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}4y\,dx+5x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5-4)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\text{Area}(D) \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 4}{2}-\frac{2\cdot 2}{2} \\  & =8-2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:

$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented. 

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i-4\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\cdot (-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡2t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/5a/5ac051f640c2b4eae760eee9c567ec35ce3169384ec2305554e21c6d2d587bbe.png)

Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $\text{curl}\,F=0$

II. $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$

III. $\text{curl}\,F$ points in the negative $z$-direction.

IV. $F$ is irrotational
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

![](images/80/80c67e624f960147b7980ee90700be800a414ab1e2a2e47faf7e8821ee0c0623.png)

If $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement II is true, whereas statement I is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would rotate counterclockwise. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- Statement III is false. Using our right hand, if we wrap our fingers in the direction of rotation (counterclockwise), our thumb will point away from the screen. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F$ also points away from the screen, in the direction of increasing $z.$

- Statement IV is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not irrotational.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=(3x+2y)\,i+({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})\,j.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $F$ at the point $(-2,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x+2y) \\  & =-2x-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(-2,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(-2,1)} & =-2(-2)-2 \\  & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}+{z}^{3}.$ Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $C$ is any smooth path from $(0,-1,1)$ to $(2,1,0)$ in ${R}^{3}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

In our case, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path $C$ are $A(0,-1,1)$ and $B(2,1,0).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(2,1,0)-f(0,-1,1) \\  & =(2(1)^{2}+{0}^{3})-(0(-1)^{2}+{1}^{3}) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x))\,dx+({x}^{2}+3xy)\,dy\,?
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/48/4822bfa926feccb0a12c14580ac325f4f10a0e4f815d0247b2231bf08b8c2326.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x)$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+3xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x+3y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x))\,dx+({x}^{2}+3xy)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+3y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.

Now, since 

$$
