question.:question/problem: Let $p=\langle2,0,-1\rangle$, $q=\langle-2,-3,-1\rangle$, and $r=\langle-1,0,-2\rangle$. Find $r\cdot(q\times p)$ using a determinant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The determinant rows follow the order in $r\cdot(q\times p)$: $r$, $q$, $p$.

$$
r\cdot(q\times p)=\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 & -2 \\ -2 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix}
$$

Call this determinant $D$. Expand across the first row with cofactor signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D&=(-1)\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix}-0\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix}+(-2)\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -3 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\ &=(-1)((-3)\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 0) \\ &\quad -0((-2)\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 2) \\ &\quad +(-2)((-2)\cdot 0-(-3)\cdot 2) \\ &=(-1)(3)-0(4)+(-2)(6) \\ &=-3+0-12 \\ &=-15.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $a=\langle-2,3,0\rangle$, $b=\langle-2,0,-1\rangle$, and $c=\langle3,1,-1\rangle$. Find $a\cdot(c\times b)$ using a determinant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The determinant rows follow the order in $a\cdot(c\times b)$: $a$, $c$, $b$.

$$
a\cdot(c\times b)=\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix}
$$

Call this determinant $D$. Expand across the first row with cofactor signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D&=(-2)\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{vmatrix}+0\begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\ &=(-2)(1\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 0) \\ &\quad -3(3\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot (-2)) \\ &\quad +0(3\cdot 0-1\cdot (-2)) \\ &=(-2)(-1)-3(-5)+0(2) \\ &=2+15+0 \\ &=17.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant rows follow the order in $b\cdot(c\times a)$: $b$, $c$, $a$.

$$
b\cdot(c\times a)=\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 \\ -2 & 3 & 2\end{vmatrix}
$$

Call this determinant $D$. Expand across the first row with cofactor signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D&=0\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 3 & 2\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\ &=0(2\cdot 2-0\cdot 3) \\ &\quad -3(2\cdot 2-0\cdot (-2)) \\ &\quad +2(2\cdot 3-2\cdot (-2)) \\ &=0(4)-3(4)+2(10) \\ &=0-12+20 \\ &=8.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant rows follow the order in $w\cdot(v\times u)$: $w$, $v$, $u$.

$$
w\cdot(v\times u)=\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 & -2 \\ -3 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 & -1\end{vmatrix}
$$

Call this determinant $D$. Expand across the first row with cofactor signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D&=3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{vmatrix}-0\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{vmatrix}+(-2)\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ -3 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ &=3(0\cdot (-1)-1\cdot (-2)) \\ &\quad -0((-3)\cdot (-1)-1\cdot (-3)) \\ &\quad +(-2)((-3)\cdot (-2)-0\cdot (-3)) \\ &=3(2)-0(6)+(-2)(6) \\ &=6+0-12 \\ &=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant rows follow the order in $r\cdot(q\times p)$: $r$, $q$, $p$.

$$
r\cdot(q\times p)=\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & -3 & -2\end{vmatrix}
$$

Call this determinant $D$. Expand across the first row with cofactor signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D&=0\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ -3 & -2\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -3 & -2\end{vmatrix}+(-1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -3 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\ &=0((-3)\cdot (-2)-0\cdot (-3)) \\ &\quad -2(1\cdot (-2)-0\cdot (-3)) \\ &\quad +(-1)(1\cdot (-3)-(-3)\cdot (-3)) \\ &=0(6)-2(-2)+(-1)(-12) \\ &=0+4+12 \\ &=16.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant rows follow the order in $c\cdot(a\times b)$: $c$, $a$, $b$.

$$
c\cdot(a\times b)=\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 3 & -3 \\ 2 & 1 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}
$$

Call this determinant $D$. Expand across the first row with cofactor signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D&=(-2)\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -3 & 2\end{vmatrix}+(-3)\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=(-2)(1\cdot 2-(-2)\cdot 1) \\ &\quad -3(2\cdot 2-(-2)\cdot (-3)) \\ &\quad +(-3)(2\cdot 1-1\cdot (-3)) \\ &=(-2)(4)-3(-2)+(-3)(5) \\ &=-8+6-15 \\ &=-17.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant rows follow the order in $v\cdot(w\times u)$: $v$, $w$, $u$.

$$
v\cdot(w\times u)=\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 3 & -3 \\ 2 & 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}
$$

Call this determinant $D$. Expand across the first row with cofactor signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D&=3\begin{vmatrix}3 & -3 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}-(-1)\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -3 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 3 \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ &=3(3\cdot 1-(-3)\cdot 2) \\ &\quad -(-1)((-3)\cdot 1-(-3)\cdot 2) \\ &\quad +2((-3)\cdot 2-3\cdot 2) \\ &=3(9)-(-1)(3)+2(-12) \\ &=27+3-24 \\ &=6.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant rows follow the order in $u\cdot(w\times v)$: $u$, $w$, $v$.

$$
u\cdot(w\times v)=\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 2\end{vmatrix}
$$

Call this determinant $D$. Expand across the first row with cofactor signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D&=3\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix}-(-2)\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ &=3(1\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot (-2)) \\ &\quad -(-2)((-1)\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 2) \\ &\quad +3((-1)\cdot (-2)-1\cdot 2) \\ &=3(0)-(-2)(0)+3(0) \\ &=0+0+0 \\ &=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant rows follow the order in $r\cdot(p\times q)$: $r$, $p$, $q$.

$$
r\cdot(p\times q)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}
$$

Call this determinant $D$. Expand across the first row with cofactor signs $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D&=1\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ &=1(1\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot 1) \\ &\quad -3(3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot 2) \\ &\quad +2(3\cdot 1-1\cdot 2) \\ &=1(2)-3(5)+2(1) \\ &=2-15+2 \\ &=-11.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field

$$
\mathbf F=\ln(x+2y)\,\mathbf i+xe^{2y}\,\mathbf j.
$$

Evaluate $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F$ at the point $(1,0)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For $\mathbf F=P\,\mathbf i+Q\,\mathbf j$, use

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

Differentiate before evaluating at the point. The other coordinate is held constant in each derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla\cdot\mathbf F
&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\ln(x+2y)+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(xe^{2y})\\
&=\frac{1}{x+2y}+2xe^{2y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The logarithm requires $x+2y>0$, which holds at $(1,0)$. Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)(1,0)
&=\frac{1}{1+2(0)}+2(1)e^{2(0)}\\
&=1+2\\
&=3.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field

$$
\mathbf F=xe^{xy}\,\mathbf i+y\ln(x+y)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Evaluate $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F$ at the point $(2,1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The divergence is a scalar:

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

Both components require the product rule. In the first derivative, hold $y$ constant and use $\partial(xy)/\partial x=y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}
&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(xe^{xy})\\
&=e^{xy}+xye^{xy}.
\end{aligned}
$$

In the second derivative, hold $x$ constant and differentiate the logarithm using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\bigl(y\ln(x+y)\bigr)\\
&=\ln(x+y)+\frac{y}{x+y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Add the derivatives before substituting. Since $2+1>0$, the point lies in the domain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla\cdot\mathbf F
&=(1+xy)e^{xy}+\ln(x+y)+\frac{y}{x+y},\\
(\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)(2,1)
&=(1+2\cdot1)e^{2\cdot1}+\ln(2+1)+\frac{1}{2+1}\\
&=3e^2+\ln 3+\frac{1}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

&=2x^2+3y^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\operatorname{div} F=\nabla\cdot F$ denotes divergence. A local excess of outward flow means positive divergence (**source**); inward flow means negative divergence (**sink**); balanced flow means zero divergence.

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

A field is **solenoidal** exactly when its divergence is zero everywhere.

The $y$-component increases as we move in the positive $y$-direction. The $x$-component is constant, so its flux across opposite sides balances. Thus there is a local excess of outward flow everywhere.

Therefore, $\nabla\cdot F>0$ everywhere, and $F$ is not solenoidal.

The true statements are $\nabla\cdot F>0$.

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field

$$
\mathbf F=\left(x e^{y}\right)\,\mathbf i+\left(2 x y e^{y}\right)\,\mathbf j.
$$

Evaluate $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F$ at the point $(-1,1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For $\mathbf F=P\,\mathbf i+Q\,\mathbf j$, use $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=P_x+Q_y$. Hold the other coordinate constant in each partial derivative.

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_x&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(x e^{y}\right)\\
&=e^{y}\\
Q_y&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(2 x y e^{y}\right)\\
&=2 x y e^{y} + 2 x e^{y}\\
\nabla\cdot\mathbf F&=P_x+Q_y
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate after differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\nabla\cdot\mathbf F)(-1,1)&=e+\left(- 4 e\right)\\
&=- 3 e.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
For $\mathbf F=P\,\mathbf i+Q\,\mathbf j$, use $\nabla\cdot\mathbf F=P_x+Q_y$. Hold the other coordinate constant in each partial derivative.

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_x&=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(x \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\right)\\
&=\frac{x^{2}}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}} + \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\\
Q_y&=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(- y \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\right)\\
&=- \frac{y^{2}}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}} - \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\\
\nabla\cdot\mathbf F&=P_x+Q_y
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate after differentiating:

$$

&=- \frac{7}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the outward flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)=(x^3+y)\,\mathbf i+(x+y)\,\mathbf j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t)=2\cos t\,\mathbf i+\sin t\,\mathbf j$ for $0\leq t\leq 2\pi$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The parametrization traverses $C$ once counterclockwise, so the outward flux is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\\
&=\int_0^{2\pi}(P y'-Q x')\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $P$ and $Q$ are evaluated at $(x(t),y(t))$.

Along $C$, $x=2\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
P&=8\cos^3t+\sin t, & Q&=2\cos t+\sin t,\\
x'(t)&=-2\sin t, & y'(t)&=\cos t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
P y'-Q x'&=(8\cos^3t+\sin t)\cos t\\
&\quad-(2\cos t+\sin t)(-2\sin t)\\
&=8\cos^4t+5\sin t\cos t+2\sin^2t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Reduce the fourth power by applying the cosine double-angle identity twice:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos^4t&=\left(\frac{1+\cos(2t)}2\right)^2\\
&=\frac14\left(1+2\cos(2t)+\frac{1+\cos(4t)}2\right)\\
&=\frac{3+4\cos(2t)+\cos(4t)}8.
\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $2\sin^2t=1-\cos(2t)$ and $5\sin t\cos t=\frac52\sin(2t)$. Substituting and collecting terms gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left(4+3\cos(2t)+\cos(4t)+\frac52\sin(2t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\left[4t+\frac32\sin(2t)+\frac14\sin(4t)-\frac54\cos(2t)\right]_0^{2\pi}\\
&=\left(8\pi-\frac54\right)-\left(-\frac54\right)=8\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the outward flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)=(x+y)\,\mathbf i+(x+2y)\,\mathbf j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t)=2\cos t\,\mathbf i+\sin t\,\mathbf j$ for $0\leq t\leq 2\pi$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The parametrization traverses $C$ once counterclockwise, so the outward flux is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\\
&=\int_0^{2\pi}(P y'-Q x')\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $P$ and $Q$ are evaluated at $(x(t),y(t))$.

Along $C$, $x=2\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
P&=2\cos t+\sin t, & Q&=2\cos t+2\sin t,\\
x'(t)&=-2\sin t, & y'(t)&=\cos t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute into the flux integrand and collect terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P y'-Q x'&=(2\cos t+\sin t)\cos t\\
&\quad-(2\cos t+2\sin t)(-2\sin t)\\
&=2\cos^2t+5\sin t\cos t+4\sin^2t.
\end{aligned}
$$

The squared terms have different coefficients, so their sum is not constant. Use $\cos^2t=(1+\cos(2t))/2$, $\sin^2t=(1-\cos(2t))/2$, and $\sin t\cos t=\sin(2t)/2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left(3-\cos(2t)+\frac52\sin(2t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\left[3t-\frac12\sin(2t)-\frac54\cos(2t)\right]_0^{2\pi}\\
&=\left(6\pi-\frac54\right)-\left(-\frac54\right)=6\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the outward flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)=(y-x)\,\mathbf i-(x+y)\,\mathbf j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t)=2\cos t\,\mathbf i+2\sin t\,\mathbf j$ for $0\leq t\leq 2\pi$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The parametrization traverses $C$ once counterclockwise, so the outward flux is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\\
&=\int_0^{2\pi}(P y'-Q x')\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $P$ and $Q$ are evaluated at $(x(t),y(t))$.

Along $C$, substitute $x=2\cos t$ and $y=2\sin t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P&=2\sin t-2\cos t, & Q&=-2\cos t-2\sin t,\\
x'(t)&=-2\sin t, & y'(t)&=2\cos t.
\end{aligned}
$$

The two mixed terms cancel. Using $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
P y'-Q x'&=(2\sin t-2\cos t)(2\cos t)\\
&\quad-(-2\cos t-2\sin t)(-2\sin t)\\
&=-4\cos^2t-4\sin^2t=-4.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Phi=\int_0^{2\pi}-4\,\mathrm{d}t=[-4t]_0^{2\pi}=-8\pi.
$$

The negative sign means that the net flow is inward.

Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F(x,y)=y\,\mathbf i+2x\,\mathbf j$ through the curve $C$ parameterized by $\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+t^2\,\mathbf j$, $0\le t\le1$, with respect to the unit normal $\mathbf n$ shown.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For $\mathbf F=P\,\mathbf i+Q\,\mathbf j$ and a parameterization $\mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t))$, evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the curve. Then

$$
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds
=\int_a^b\left(Py'-Qx'\right)\mathrm dt,
$$

provided $\mathbf n$ is the $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent for increasing $t$.

For increasing $t$, the curve runs from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$, with tangent direction $(1,2t)$. Its clockwise normal direction is $(2t,-1)$, agreeing with the pictured normal, so we may use the formula directly.

![Tangent and clockwise normal](images/46/4697accf510b0ea92f64022a1a6f75077d38bf2eed0273ca8a80cf8fb174567c.png)

Substitute the curve into both components of the field and differentiate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=t,&y&=t^2,\\
P&=y=t^2,&Q&=2x=2t,\\
x'&=1,&y'&=2t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds
&=\int_0^1\left[(t^2)(2t)-(2t)(1)\right]\mathrm dt\\
&=\int_0^1(2t^3-2t)\,\mathrm dt\\
&=\left[\frac{t^4}{2}-t^2\right]_0^1\\
&=\frac12-1=-\frac12.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

=\int_a^b\left(Py'-Qx'\right)\mathrm dt,
$$

provided $\mathbf n$ is the $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent for increasing $t$.

Choose $y=t$, so $x=t^2$ and $0\le t\le2$. This parameterization starts at $(0,0)$ and ends at $(4,2)$. Its tangent direction is $(2t,1)$; rotating clockwise gives $(1,-2t)$, agreeing with the pictured normal.

$$

$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the supplied parameterization $x=\frac{1}{t},\ y=t$, $\frac{1}{2}\le t\le 2$. It runs from $(2,\frac{1}{2})$ to $(\frac{1}{2},2)$.

The tangent has direction $(- \frac{1}{t^{2}},1)$. The pictured normal is its $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation, with direction $(1,\frac{1}{t^{2}})$.

![Tangent and selected normal](images/67/670abe5e761fb3e80045bf6cf153979daa6ce099ecca125621749d794dcc534d.png)

Substitute the curve into the field and differentiate its coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x(t),y(t))&=- 4 \left(\frac{1}{t}\right)=- \frac{4}{t} \\
Q(x(t),y(t))&=2 \left(t\right)^{2}=2 t^{2} \\
x'&=- \frac{1}{t^{2}} \\
y'&=1\end{aligned}
$$

The clockwise normal permits the flux formula directly.

At positive endpoints use $\ln(1/u)=-\ln u$, $\ln u-\ln v=\ln(u/v)$, and $\ln e=1$ as needed; retain the logarithm terms in the final value.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm ds&=\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{2}(Py\prime-Qx\prime)\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{2}\left[\left(- \frac{4}{t}\right)(1)-(2 t^{2})\left(- \frac{1}{t^{2}}\right)\right]\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{2}(2 - \frac{4}{t})\,\mathrm dt \\
&=\left[2 t - 4 \ln{\left(t \right)}\right]_{\frac{1}{2}}^{2} \\
&=(4 - 4 \ln{\left(2 \right)})-(1 + 4 \ln{\left(2 \right)}) \\
&=3 - 8 \ln{\left(2 \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve in $\mathbb{R}^2$, and let $D$ be the region it encloses. Which of the following vector fields make

$$
\oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}=\operatorname{Area}(D)
$$

for every such curve?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $\mathbf{F}=\langle P,Q\rangle$. Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y
=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

All the displayed functions have continuous first partial derivatives on $\mathbb{R}^2$. To give area for every such region, the scalar curl must be identically $1$. We differentiate with respect to the indicated variable, holding the other variable constant.

For the first field,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=e^y-1,\\
Q_x&=e^y,\\
Q_x-P_y&=e^y-(e^y-1)=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

So select the first field. The term $y^2$ in $Q$ is constant with respect to $x$.

For the second field,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=\sin x,\\
Q_x&=1-\sin x,\\
Q_x-P_y&=1-2\sin x.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is not identically $1$, so do not select this field. Its curl equals $1$ when $x=0$, but equality at a few points does not meet the requirement for every region.

For the third field,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=-\frac14,\\
Q_x&=\frac34,\\
Q_x-P_y&=\frac34-\left(-\frac14\right)=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The terms $\cos(x^2)$ in $P$ and $y^3$ in $Q$ disappear in these partial derivatives. Select the third field.

Therefore, select the **first and third fields**.

question.:question/problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve in $\mathbb{R}^2$, and let $D$ be the region it encloses. Which of the following pairs of functions make

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y=\operatorname{Area}(D)
$$

for every such curve?

I. $P(x,y)=y+x^2$ and $Q(x,y)=x+y^2$

II. $P(x,y)=-y+x^2$ and $Q(x,y)=y^2$

III. $P(x,y)=2y$ and $Q(x,y)=3x+y^2$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y
=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

All the displayed functions have continuous first partial derivatives on $\mathbb{R}^2$. To give area for every such region, the scalar curl must be identically $1$. We differentiate with respect to the indicated variable, holding the other variable constant.

- **I:** $P_y=1$ and $Q_x=1$, so $Q_x-P_y=1-1=0$. This pair does not give area.
- **II:** $P_y=-1$ and $Q_x=0$, so $Q_x-P_y=0-(-1)=1$. This pair gives area.
- **III:** $P_y=2$ and $Q_x=3$, so $Q_x-P_y=3-2=1$. This pair also gives area.

The $x^2$ terms in $P$ and the $y^2$ terms in $Q$ disappear in the required partial derivatives. Therefore, the answer is **II and III only**.

question.:question/problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve in $\mathbb{R}^2$, and let $D$ be the region it encloses. Which of the following vector fields make

$$
\oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}=\operatorname{Area}(D)
$$

for every such curve?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $\mathbf{F}=\langle P,Q\rangle$. Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y
=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

All the displayed functions have continuous first partial derivatives on $\mathbb{R}^2$. To give area for every such region, the scalar curl must be identically $1$. We differentiate with respect to the indicated variable, holding the other variable constant.

For the first field, use both the product and chain rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=\sin(xy)+xy\cos(xy)-1,\\
Q_x&=\sin(xy)+xy\cos(xy),\\
Q_x-P_y&=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The two variable terms cancel, leaving $1$. Select this field.

For the second field,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=e^{xy}+xy e^{xy}-\frac12,\\
Q_x&=e^{xy}+xy e^{xy}+\frac12,\\
Q_x-P_y&=\frac12-\left(-\frac12\right)=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Again, both variable terms cancel. Select this field.

For the third field,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=\sin(xy)+xy\cos(xy)-1,\\
Q_x&=\sin(xy)+xy\cos(xy)+2x,\\
Q_x-P_y&=1+2x.
\end{aligned}
$$

The trigonometric terms cancel, but $2x$ remains. This curl is not identically $1$; for example, it is $3$ at $x=1$. Do not select this field. Agreement on the line $x=0$ is insufficient for every region in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

Therefore, select the **first and second fields**.

question.:question/problem:

Let $D$ be enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized by
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle e^{\cos t},e^{\sin t}\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le 2\pi.
$$
Using $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0$, the area can be written as
$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm dA
=\int_0^{2\pi} f(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$
Which expression is the pointwise integrand obtained from this $P$, $Q$ and parametrization using Green's theorem, with the sign appropriate to the orientation shown? Do not evaluate the integral.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The diagram shows a counterclockwise boundary. This also follows from the parametrization: at $t=0$ it starts at $(e,1)$ and moves upward. The map $(u,v)\mapsto(e^u,e^v)$ preserves the orientation and simplicity of the unit circle.

The chosen field has scalar curl
$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$
Green's theorem therefore gives
$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\oint_C(-y)\,\mathrm dx.
$$
Differentiate $x(t)$ by the chain rule:
$$
x^{\prime}(t)=-\sin t\,e^{\cos t}.
$$
Substituting both the coefficient and the differential gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
f(t)&=-y(t)x^{\prime}(t)\\
&=-e^{\sin t}\left(-\sin t\,e^{\cos t}\right)\\
&=\sin t\,e^{\cos t+\sin t}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Hence the required setup is
$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\int_0^{2\pi}\sin t\,e^{\cos t+\sin t}\,\mathrm dt.
$$
Using $x\,\mathrm dy$ instead would give a different pointwise integrand. That belongs to the other unit-curl field $P=0$, $Q=x$, rather than the field specified here.

:answer-field/choices.:answer/feedback: Clockwise orientation requires negating $x(t)y^{\prime}(t)$, cancelling its minus sign.
The derivative of $\cos t$ supplies another factor of $\sin t$.
This comes from $y(t)x^{\prime}(t)$. The given $P=0$, $Q=x$ requires $-x(t)y^{\prime}(t)$.
The power rule supplies a factor of $5$.
Correct: $-(\sin^5 t)(-5\cos^4 t\sin t)=5\sin^6 t\cos^4 t$.

Let $D$ be enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized by
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle\sin^5 t,\cos^5 t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le 2\pi.
$$
Using $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x$, the area can be written as
$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm dA
=\int_0^{2\pi} f(t)\,\mathrm dt.
$$
Which expression is the pointwise integrand obtained from this $P$, $Q$ and parametrization using Green's theorem, with its sign adjusted for the orientation of $C$? Do not evaluate the integral.

*Hint: $C$ is negatively oriented.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
The curve is simple and piecewise smooth, with cusps at its axis intercepts. It is traversed clockwise. For the given field,
$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=1-0=1.
$$
Because the orientation is negative, area is the negative of the circulation:
$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=-\oint_C\left(P\,\mathrm dx+Q\,\mathrm dy\right)=-\oint_C x\,\mathrm dy.
$$
The chain rule gives
$$
y^{\prime}(t)=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(\cos^5 t)=-5\cos^4 t\sin t.
$$
Substitute into the orientation-adjusted expression:
$$
\begin{aligned}
f(t)&=-x(t)y^{\prime}(t)\\
&=-(\sin^5 t)(-5\cos^4 t\sin t)\\
&=5\sin^6 t\cos^4 t.
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus
$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\int_0^{2\pi}5\sin^6 t\cos^4 t\,\mathrm dt.
$$
One minus sign comes from clockwise orientation and the other from differentiating $\cos t$. They cancel. The powers of $\sin t$ add to $6$.

:answer-field/choices.:answer/feedback: Correct: $(3\cos t)(2\cos t)=6\cos^2 t$.
The boundary is positively oriented, so there is no extra minus sign.
Include the factor $2$ from $y^{\prime}(t)$.
Use the supplied $y^{\prime}(t)=2\cos t$, not $y(t)=2\sin t$.
Multiply $x(t)$ by $y^{\prime}(t)$, not by $y(t)$.

$$
Here $x(t)=3\cos t$ and $y^{\prime}(t)=2\cos t$.

Which expression is the pointwise integrand $f(t)=x(t)y^{\prime}(t)$? Do not evaluate the integral.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For this counterclockwise boundary, Green's theorem applies with a positive sign because
$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=1-0=1.
$$
In $\oint_C x\,\mathrm dy$, replace $x$ by $x(t)$ and $\mathrm dy$ by $y^{\prime}(t)\,\mathrm dt$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
f(t)&=(3\cos t)(2\cos t)\\
&=6\cos^2 t.
\end{aligned}
$$
Therefore
$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\int_0^{2\pi}6\cos^2 t\,\mathrm dt.
$$
The requested expression is $6\cos^2 t$. Although $6\sin^2 t$ has the same integral over this interval, it is not the pointwise product $x(t)y^{\prime}(t)$.

question.:question/problem:
The curve $C$ is parametrized by
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 2\cos t,\sin t\rangle,\qquad 0\leq t\leq 2\pi.
$$
It traverses the boundary of $D$ once counterclockwise. Use Green's theorem with $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0$ to find the area of $D$.

![The ellipse with intercepts (plus or minus 2, 0) and (0, plus or minus 1), traversed counterclockwise.](images/29/29f6e1c802a936c7f5a2fb8d55ff228dc1504a00ea663710f43d4880d2b4cfca.png)
question.:question/worked-solution:
The chosen field has unit scalar curl:
$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$
Since $C$ is positively oriented, Green's theorem gives
$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=\iint_D 1\,dA=-\oint_C y\,dx.
$$
Here $y(t)=\sin t$ and $x'(t)=-2\sin t$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Area}(D)&=-\int_0^{2\pi}\sin t(-2\sin t)\,dt\\
&=\int_0^{2\pi}(1-\cos 2t)\,dt\\
&=\left[t-\tfrac12\sin 2t\right]_0^{2\pi}\\
&=2\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$
The area is $2\pi$ square units.

question.:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve
$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle\sin t,\sin 2t\rangle,\qquad 0\leq t\leq\pi.
$$
The arrows indicate the direction of increasing $t$.

![A loop to the right of the y-axis, from the origin along its upper branch and back along its lower branch, with clockwise arrows.](images/9f/9f80d82b0d4c4c7e7d8d59ffbbd059fa57d02d254af79b514cdef81a5a81d816.png)
question.:question/worked-solution:
The path starts at $(0,0)$, follows the upper branch to $(1,0)$, and returns along the lower branch. It is clockwise, so it has negative orientation.

Choose $P=-y$ and $Q=0$. Their scalar curl is $1$. Green's theorem with the orientation correction gives
$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=-\oint_C(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=\oint_C y\,dx.
$$
Since $x'(t)=\cos t$ and $y(t)=\sin 2t$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Area}(D)&=\int_0^\pi\sin 2t\cos t\,dt\\
&=2\int_0^\pi\sin t\cos^2t\,dt.
\end{aligned}
$$
Set $u=\cos t$, so $du=-\sin t\,dt$. The limits become $1$ and $-1$. Hence
$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=-2\int_1^{-1}u^2\,du
=\frac{2}{3}\left[u^3\right]_{-1}^{1}
=\frac{4}{3}.
$$
The area is $\frac43$ square units. Using $-\oint_C y\,dx$ without correcting the clockwise orientation would give the negative of the area.

question.:question/problem:
The boundary $C=C_1\cup C_2$ encloses a region $D$, where

- $C_1$ is parametrized by $\mathbf r_1(t)=\langle t^3,-t^4\rangle$ for $-1\leq t\leq1$;
- $C_2$ is parametrized by $\mathbf r_2(t)=\langle-t,-1\rangle$ for $-1\leq t\leq1$.

Traverse $C_1$ and then $C_2$ in the directions of increasing parameter. Use Green's theorem to find the area of $D$.

![The curved upper boundary C1 runs from (-1,-1) through (0,0) to (1,-1). The horizontal lower boundary C2 returns to (-1,-1).](images/d5/d58009320fabb8ea68bbc67a0c62198965cd5297ba287f5e27e8d45d064269eb.png)
question.:question/worked-solution:
The endpoints join: $C_1$ goes from $(-1,-1)$ to $(1,-1)$ through $(0,0)$, and $C_2$ returns from $(1,-1)$ to $(-1,-1)$. The boundary is clockwise.

Choose $P=0$ and $Q=x$, whose scalar curl is $1$. Because the orientation is negative,
$$
\operatorname{Area}(D)=-\oint_C x\,dy
=-\int_{C_1}x\,dy-\int_{C_2}x\,dy.
$$
On $C_1$, $x=t^3$ and $dy=-4t^3\,dt$. On $C_2$, $y=-1$ is constant, so $dy=0$. Therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Area}(D)&=-\int_{-1}^1t^3(-4t^3)\,dt-\int_{-1}^1(-t)\cdot0\,dt\\
&=4\int_{-1}^1t^6\,dt\\
&=4\left[\frac{t^7}{7}\right]_{-1}^1\\
&=4\left(\frac17+\frac17\right)=\frac87.
\end{aligned}
$$
The straight segment contributes zero for this choice of field; it is still needed to close the boundary. The area is $\frac87$ square units.

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the outward flux of

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\langle x+\sin y,\ y+\cos x\rangle
$$

through the boundary of

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le1,\ 0\le y\le x^2\}.
$$

![Region below y=x squared, above y=0, between x=0 and x=1.](images/35/3572e500529bb0e2e4a21ed94d0f31a1b5edc3406a572d7173225f4fc440a606.png)

For $\mathbf F=\langle P,Q\rangle$, use

$$
\Phi=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

Select the flux.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The components have continuous first derivatives on an open set containing $D$. With $C=\partial D$ traversed counterclockwise and $\mathbf n$ pointing outward, Green's theorem in flux form gives

$$
\Phi=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds
=\oint_C P\,dy-Q\,dx
=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

Here $P=x+\sin y$ and $Q=y+\cos x$, so

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=1,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=1.
$$

Thus the divergence is $2$. The supplied bounds describe a type I region. Integrating first with respect to $y$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_0^1\int_0^{x^2}2\,dy\,dx\\
&=\int_0^1[2y]_{y=0}^{y=x^2}\,dx\\
&=\int_0^1 2x^2\,dx\\
&=\left[\frac{2x^3}{3}\right]_0^1=\frac{2}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The outward flux is $\frac{2}{3}$.

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the outward flux of

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\langle x^2+\sin y,\ xy+e^x\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by $y=x^3$, $y=0$, and $x=1$.

Select the flux.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The components have continuous first derivatives on an open set containing $D$. With $C=\partial D$ traversed counterclockwise and $\mathbf n$ pointing outward, Green's theorem in flux form gives

$$
\Phi=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds
=\oint_C P\,dy-Q\,dx
=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

Here $P=x^2+\sin y$ and $Q=xy+e^x$, so

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=2x,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=x.
$$

The divergence is $3x$. The curve $y=x^3$ meets $y=0$ at $x=0$. From there to $x=1$, the region lies above $y=0$ and below $y=x^3$:

![Region below y=x cubed, above y=0, and left of x=1.](images/26/26cbf8624da7845c8c2022254893e53b6dc85561f9878dc5989d11eaad035bac.png)

Hence its type I description is

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le1,\ 0\le y\le x^3\}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_0^1\int_0^{x^3}3x\,dy\,dx\\
&=\int_0^1[3xy]_{y=0}^{y=x^3}\,dx\\
&=\int_0^1 3x^4\,dx\\
&=\left[\frac{3x^5}{5}\right]_0^1=\frac{3}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The outward flux is $\frac{3}{5}$.

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the outward flux of

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\langle x^2+\sin y,\ xy+e^x\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by $x=-2y$, $x=\sqrt{y}$, and $y=1$.

Select the flux.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The components have continuous first derivatives on an open set containing $D$. With $C=\partial D$ traversed counterclockwise and $\mathbf n$ pointing outward, Green's theorem in flux form gives

$$
\Phi=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds
=\oint_C P\,dy-Q\,dx
=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

Here $P=x^2+\sin y$ and $Q=xy+e^x$, so

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=2x,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=x.
$$

The divergence is $3x$. Since $\sqrt{y}\ge0$ and $-2y\le0$ for $y\ge0$, the two curves meet only at $(0,0)$. The top boundary is $y=1$. A horizontal slice runs from $x=-2y$ to $x=\sqrt{y}$:

![Region between x=-2y on the left and x=square root of y on the right, from y=0 to y=1; a horizontal slice is shown.](images/6e/6e28b8a2920142f7847d2813fc350248b8bbdf4c1fced6d89ba823ce778e483a.png)

Thus a type II description avoids splitting the region:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le y\le1,\ -2y\le x\le\sqrt{y}\}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_0^1\int_{-2y}^{\sqrt{y}}3x\,dx\,dy\\
&=\int_0^1\left[\frac{3x^2}{2}\right]_{x=-2y}^{x=\sqrt{y}}\,dy\\
&=\frac{3}{2}\int_0^1(y-4y^2)\,dy\\
&=\frac{3}{2}\left[\frac{y^2}{2}-\frac{4y^3}{3}\right]_0^1\\
&=\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac12-\frac43\right)=-\frac54.
\end{aligned}
$$

The outward flux is $-\frac54$. Its negative sign means the net flux points into the region. The left side's negative contribution outweighs the right side's positive contribution; the region is not symmetric about the $y$-axis.

question.:question/problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0)$, $(2,0)$, $(2,1)$, and $(-1,1)$, traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the outward flux of

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\langle x^2y+xy^2,\,-xy^2+y^3\rangle
$$

through $C$ as a repeated integral. Do not evaluate the integral.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For $\mathbf F=\langle P,Q\rangle$, the flux form of Green's theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s
&=\oint_C\left(P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\right)\\
&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial components have continuous first derivatives on a neighborhood of $D$, and the counterclockwise boundary has the required positive orientation.

The region $D$ and its boundary $C$ are shown below.

![Rectangle with horizontal range -1 to 2 and vertical range 0 to 1.](images/a4/a418f22532577cce1962726ecf6ed61537b25c2df0c71de395ccdef462d68e55.png)

The component derivatives are

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=2xy+y^2,\qquad
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=-2xy+3y^2.
$$

Adding, rather than subtracting, cancels the mixed terms:

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=4y^2.
$$

The rectangle is $D=\{(x,y):-1\leq x\leq2,\ 0\leq y\leq1\}$. Integrating with respect to $y$ first gives

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s
=\int_{-1}^{2}\int_0^1 4y^2\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

The inner bounds belong to $y$ and the outer bounds belong to $x$.

question.:question/problem:
Let $C$ be the boundary of the finite region enclosed by the parabolas $y=x^2$ and $y=2-x^2$, traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the outward flux of

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\langle x^2y+xy,\,-xy^2+y^2\rangle
$$

through $C$ as a repeated integral in the order $\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x$. Do not evaluate the integral.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For $\mathbf F=\langle P,Q\rangle$, the flux form of Green's theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s
&=\oint_C\left(P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\right)\\
&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial components have continuous first derivatives on a neighborhood of $D$, and the counterclockwise boundary has the required positive orientation.

First find where the boundaries meet:

$$
x^2=2-x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^2=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=-1\text{ or }x=1.
$$

Both intersection points have $y=1$. Between these $x$-values, the lower boundary is $y=x^2$ and the upper boundary is $y=2-x^2$.

![Region between an upward parabola and a downward parabola, meeting at (-1,1) and (1,1).](images/1e/1ea32c48979cb2b4e5370b599d184b16ab1f37525b886c2ce3161f459c0232d6.png)

Consequently,

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\leq x\leq1,\ x^2\leq y\leq2-x^2\}.
$$

For the field components,

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=2xy+y,\qquad
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=-2xy+2y,
$$

so the divergence is $3y$. Combining this integrand with the bounds in the requested order gives

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s
=\int_{-1}^{1}\int_{x^2}^{2-x^2}3y\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

Using constant bounds $0\leq y\leq2$ would instead include points outside the curved region.

question.:question/problem:

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\langle x^2+y^3,\,2xy+y^2\rangle
$$

across the triangle $C$ with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, and $(0,2)$ can be represented as

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s=\iint_D f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $\mathbf n$ is the outward unit normal, and $D$ is the enclosed region. Calculate $f(x,y)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For $\mathbf F=\langle P,Q\rangle$, the flux form of Green's theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s
&=\oint_C\left(P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\right)\\
&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial components have continuous first derivatives on a neighborhood of $D$, and the counterclockwise boundary has the required positive orientation.

The region is shown below.

![The triangular region bounded by the coordinate axes and the line through (1,0) and (0,2).](images/c3/c3c617522488e6ebf47dd2b2a52c43a1fe06ccaef8cd1e8752ab4df5e2d4bd64.png)

Here $P=x^2+y^3$ and $Q=2xy+y^2$. Differentiate each component with respect to its matching coordinate:

$$

$$

$$

$$

The triangle specifies the integration region; its bounds are not needed to find the integrand.

$$

for every such curve?

Select all that apply.

$$

**II.**

$$
\mathbf{F}_{II}(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}x^{2} - 2 y \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\\x + \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\end{pmatrix}
$$

**III.**

$$
\mathbf{F}_{III}(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}x + 2 y \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + \frac{y}{2}\\\frac{3 x}{2} + \sin{\left(y \right)} - \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\end{pmatrix}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $\mathbf{F}=\langle P,Q\rangle$. Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y
=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

All the displayed functions have continuous first partial derivatives on $\mathbb{R}^2$. For the circulation to equal area for every such region, the scalar curl must be identically $1$. Hold the other coordinate constant in each partial derivative.

**I.** 

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=e^{x + 2 y} - 1,\\
Q_x&=- e^{x + 2 y},\\
Q_x-P_y&=\left(- e^{x + 2 y}\right)\\
&\quad-\left(e^{x + 2 y} - 1\right)\\
&=- 2 e^{x} e^{2 y} + 1.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is not identically $1$: at $(x,y)=(0,0)$ its value is $-1$. Do not select **I**.

**II.** 

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=- 2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)},\\
Q_x&=- 2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 1,\\
Q_x-P_y&=\left(- 2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + 1\right)\\
&\quad-\left(- 2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\right)\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The scalar curl is identically $1$, so select **II**.

**III.** 

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + \frac{1}{2},\\
Q_x&=2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + \frac{3}{2},\\
Q_x-P_y&=\left(2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + \frac{3}{2}\right)\\
&\quad-\left(2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + \frac{1}{2}\right)\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The scalar curl is identically $1$, so select **III**.

Therefore, select **II and III only**.

$$

Thus the missing pointwise expression is $\left(\cos{\left(t \right)} - \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\right) \left(3 \cos{\left(t \right)} - 6 \cos{\left(2 t \right)}\right)$.

question.:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem in flux form to calculate the outward flux of

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\left\langle\sin y+2x,\ e^x-y\right\rangle
$$
through the boundary of the rectangle $D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le2,\ 0\le y\le1\}$.

For $\mathbf F=\langle P,Q\rangle$, you are given

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=2,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=-1.
$$

Use

$$
\Phi=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $D$ be the rectangle and let $C=\partial D$ be traversed counterclockwise, with outward unit normal $\mathbf n$. The components $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D$. Green's theorem in flux form gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s\\
&=\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\\
&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
\end{aligned}
$$

The rectangle $D$ and its boundary are shown below.

![Rectangle from x equals 0 to 2 and y equals 0 to 1](images/ea/ea6c25e40b6683d9ff4a4884dbbda708fd79dbd79d0b50730f9ad6e165d2eb58.png)

The term $\sin y$ is constant when differentiating $P$ with respect to $x$, and $e^x$ is constant when differentiating $Q$ with respect to $y$. Thus the given derivatives yield divergence $2+(-1)=1$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_0^1\int_0^2(2-1)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_0^1[x]_0^2\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_0^1 2\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=[2y]_0^1=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, constant divergence $1$ times the rectangle's area $2\cdot1$ gives outward flux $2$.

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the outward flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\left\langle e^y+x^2y,\ \cos x+xy^2+2y\right\rangle
$$
through the boundary of the rectangle with vertices $(-1,0)$, $(2,0)$, $(2,1)$, and $(-1,1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $D$ be the rectangle and let $C=\partial D$ be traversed counterclockwise, with outward unit normal $\mathbf n$. The components $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D$. Green's theorem in flux form gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s\\
&=\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x\\
&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
\end{aligned}
$$

The vertices give $D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le2,\ 0\le y\le1\}$, shown below.

![Rectangle from x equals minus 1 to 2 and y equals 0 to 1](images/f6/f6437eddec7d44a10c7fb2b3461a09844ca06e5131b69503f51432eb87fedd31.png)

Here $P=e^y+x^2y$ and $Q=\cos x+xy^2+2y$. Holding the other variable constant gives

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=2xy,\qquad
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=2xy+2,
\qquad \operatorname{div}\mathbf F=4xy+2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_0^1\int_{-1}^2(4xy+2)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_0^1[2x^2y+2x]_{-1}^2\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_0^1\bigl((8y+4)-(2y-2)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_0^1(6y+6)\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=[3y^2+6y]_0^1=9.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both parts contribute: the $4xy$ term integrates to $3$, and constant divergence $2$ contributes $2$ times the rectangle's area $3$, giving $6$. Their sum is $9$.

The rectangle $D$ and its boundary are shown below.

![Rectangle from x equals 0 to 2 and y equals minus 1 to 1](images/2f/2f3374de4a29c62587a79f6286dfe788e64c37e09e9d9b83b3a67b4dac10dc21.png)

Here $P=\cos y-x^2$ and $Q=\sin x+3y$. The cross-variable terms contribute zero to the relevant partial derivatives:

The inner integral is $2$; the outer integral accounts for the full height $1-(-1)=2$.

$$

$$

$$

The components have continuous first derivatives on a neighborhood of $D$. With $C=\partial D$ counterclockwise and $\mathbf n$ outward, Green\'s theorem gives

$$
\Phi=\oint_C P\,dy-Q\,dx=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

Here $P=2 x + \sin{\left(y \right)}$ and $Q=- y + \cos{\left(x \right)}$, so

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=2,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=-1,\qquad \operatorname{div}\mathbf F=1.
$$

On the stated interval, $2 \sin{\left(x \right)}\geq0$. Use vertical slices from $y=0$ to $y=2 \sin{\left(x \right)}$.

This is a type I region:

$$

$$

Integrating and substituting both inner limits gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\Phi&=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{2 \sin{\left(x \right)}}\left(1\right)\,dy\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left[y\right]_{y=0}^{y=2 \sin{\left(x \right)}}\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left[\left(2 \sin{\left(x \right)}\right)-\left(0\right)\right]\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\left(2 \sin{\left(x \right)}\right)\,dx \\&=\left[- 2 \cos{\left(x \right)}\right]_{x=0}^{x=\frac{\pi}{2}} \\&=\left(0\right)-\left(-2\right) \\&=2.\end{aligned}
$$

The outward flux is $2$.

question.:question/worked-solution:

$$
\Phi=\oint_C P\,dy-Q\,dx=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

Here $P=- 2 x^{2} y - \cos{\left(y \right)}$ and $Q=e^{x}$, so

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}=- 4 x y,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}\mathbf F=- 4 x y.
$$

The curved boundary meets $y=0$ at the origin. Up to $x=2$, vertical slices run from $y=0$ to $y=2 \sqrt{x}$.

![Shaded region and a representative integration slice.](images/a1/a1c6dfa6dd998451b9caf7772e1b1931a780cc689c8fa301916c7498adf005f2.png)

$$

$$

Integrating and substituting both inner limits gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\Phi&=\int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{2 \sqrt{x}}\left(- 4 x y\right)\,dy\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{2}\left[- 2 x y^{2}\right]_{y=0}^{y=2 \sqrt{x}}\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{2}\left[\left(- 8 x^{2}\right)-\left(0\right)\right]\,dx \\&=\int_{0}^{2}\left(- 8 x^{2}\right)\,dx \\&=\left[- \frac{8 x^{3}}{3}\right]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\&=\left(- \frac{64}{3}\right)-\left(0\right) \\&=- \frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
For $\mathbf F=\langle P,Q\rangle$, Green's theorem in flux form states

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s
&=\oint_C(P\,\mathrm{d}y-Q\,\mathrm{d}x)\\
&=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
\end{aligned}
$$

The polynomial components have continuous first partial derivatives on a neighborhood of the enclosed region. The counterclockwise boundary has positive orientation.

The matching component derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}&=3 y^{3}\\ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}&=8 x y^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Add these derivatives to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}&=(3 y^{3})+(8 x y^{3})\\ &=8 x y^{3} + 3 y^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The rectangular coordinate ranges give

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\leq x\leq 2,\ -2\leq y\leq 0\}.
$$

Putting the integrand and bounds together in the requested order gives

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{-2}^{0}\int_{0}^{2}(8 x y^{3} + 3 y^{3})\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$

\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}&=3.
\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the matching partials gives

$$
\operatorname{div}\mathbf F=5.
$$

Integrate with respect to $x$, subtract its endpoints, then integrate with respect to $y$ and subtract its endpoints.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Phi&=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{-1}^{1}\left(5\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left[5 x\right]_{x=-1}^{x=1}\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(10\right)\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&=\left[10 y\right]_{y=0}^{y=1}\\
&=\left(10\right)-\left(0\right)\\
&=10.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=t^3-2t,\qquad y=2t^2+t,\qquad -\infty<t<\infty.
$$

Find the Cartesian equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=-1$.

The equation of the tangent line is $y=$ {{field-1}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First find the point by substituting $t=-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x(-1)&=(-1)^3-2(-1)=1,\\
y(-1)&=2(-1)^2+(-1)=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate the coordinate functions:

$$
x'(t)=3t^2-2,\qquad y'(t)=4t+1.
$$

The tangent slope is $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{4t+1}{3t^2-2}$. At $t=-1$,

$$
m=\frac{4(-1)+1}{3(-1)^2-2}=\frac{-3}{1}=-3.
$$

Use point-slope form with $(1,1)$ and slope $-3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-1&=-3(x-1),\\
y&=-3x+4.
\end{aligned}
$$

Enter $-3x+4$, the expression after $y=$.

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=t(\ln t+1),\qquad y=\ln t,\qquad t>0.
$$

Let $C$ be the point corresponding to $t=e$. Determine the coordinates of the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis. Give exact answers.

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}}$,\,${{field-2}}$)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Substitute $t=e$ to find $C$:

$$
x(e)=e(\ln e+1)=2e,\qquad y(e)=\ln e=1.
$$

Use the product rule to differentiate $x(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x'(t)&=(\ln t+1)+t\cdot\frac{1}{t}=\ln t+2,\\
y'(t)&=\frac{1}{t}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent slope at $C$ is

$$
m=\frac{y'(e)}{x'(e)}=\frac{1/e}{3}=\frac{1}{3e}.
$$

The tangent through $(2e,1)$ therefore has equation

$$
y-1=\frac{1}{3e}(x-2e).
$$

On the $y$-axis, $x=0$. Substitute this into the tangent equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-1&=\frac{1}{3e}(0-2e)=-\frac{2}{3},\\
y&=\frac{1}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the required intersection is

$$
\left(0,\frac{1}{3}\right).
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Substitute $t=-1$ to find $C$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=(-1)^4+(-1)+1=1,\\
y&=(-1)^2+1=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $C=(1,2)$. Differentiate the two coordinates:

$$
x'(t)=4t^3+1,\qquad y'(t)=2t.
$$

The tangent slope is

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2t}{4t^3+1}.
$$

Evaluate it at $t=-1$:

$$
m=\frac{2(-1)}{4(-1)^3+1}=\frac{-2}{-3}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

The slope of the normal is the negative reciprocal:

$$
m_n=-\frac{1}{2/3}=-\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Use point-slope form through $(1,2)$:

$$
y-2=-\frac{3}{2}(x-1).
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$. Substitute this and solve for $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-2&=-\frac{3}{2}(x-1),\\
x-1&=\frac{4}{3},\\
x&=\frac{7}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the normal crosses the $x$-axis at $\left(\dfrac{7}{3},0\right)$.

y-3&=-\frac{1}{2}(x-3)\\

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\ln(t^2)+1,\qquad y=2t^3-3t+3,\qquad t>0.
$$

Let $C$ be the point where $t=1$. Find the Cartesian equation of the normal to the curve at $C$. Give an exact answer.

The normal line is $y=$ {{field-1}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First find the coordinates of $C$ by substituting $t=1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=\ln(1^2)+1=1,\\
y&=2(1)^3-3(1)+3=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $C=(1,2)$. Differentiate both coordinates with respect to $t$:

$$
x'(t)=\frac{2t}{t^2}=\frac{2}{t},\qquad y'(t)=6t^2-3.
$$

The tangent slope is the ratio of these derivatives:

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{6t^2-3}{2/t}=\frac{t(6t^2-3)}{2}.
$$

At $t=1$ this gives

$$
m=\frac{6-3}{2}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Take its negative reciprocal to obtain the normal slope:

$$
m_n=-\frac{1}{3/2}=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$

The normal passes through $(1,2)$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-2&=-\frac{2}{3}(x-1),\\
y&=-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{2}{3}+2,\\
y&=-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{8}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Enter $-\dfrac{2}{3}x+\dfrac{8}{3}$ in the blank after $y=$.

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=3\cos t+1,\qquad y=2\sin t-4,\qquad 0<t<2\pi.
$$

Determine the values of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is vertical.

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a vertical tangent, we need $x'(t)=0$ while $y'(t)\ne0$. The coordinate derivatives are

$$
x'(t)=-3\sin t,\qquad y'(t)=2\cos t.
$$

Solving $x'(t)=0$ gives $\sin t=0$, so the candidates on the closed interval $[0,2\pi]$ are $0$, $\pi$, and $2\pi$. The problem specifies the open interval $0<t<2\pi$, so only $t=\pi$ remains.

Check the other derivative:

$$
y'(\pi)=2\cos\pi=-2\ne0.
$$

Thus the tangent is vertical only at $t=\pi$ on the specified interval. At $t=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $t=\frac{3\pi}{2}$, it is $y'(t)$ that is zero, while $x'(t)$ is nonzero; those tangents are horizontal.

question.:question/problem:

x=3(t+2),\qquad y=2(t-1)^2+4,\qquad -\infty<t<\infty.
$$

Determine the value of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is horizontal.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The slope of a tangent to a parametric curve is

$$
m=\frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

For a horizontal tangent, we need $y'(t)=0$ and $x'(t)\ne0$. Differentiate both coordinates:

$$
x'(t)=3,\qquad y'(t)=4(t-1).
$$

Solve for the zero of $y'(t)$:

$$
4(t-1)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t=1.
$$

Since $x'(1)=3\ne0$, the tangent is horizontal at $t=1$.

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\frac{t^2+2}{t+1},\qquad y=t^2+2t,\qquad -1<t<\infty.
$$

Determine the value of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is vertical. Give an exact answer.

The tangent to the curve is vertical at $t=${{field-1}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
A vertical tangent requires $x'(t)=0$ and $y'(t)\ne0$. Using the quotient rule for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
x'(t)&=\frac{2t(t+1)-(t^2+2)}{(t+1)^2}\\
&=\frac{t^2+2t-2}{(t+1)^2},\\
y'(t)&=2t+2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Because $t>-1$, the denominator $(t+1)^2$ is nonzero. Hence $x'(t)=0$ exactly when

$$
\begin{aligned}
t^2+2t-2&=0\\
(t+1)^2&=3\\
t&=-1\pm\sqrt{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The root $-1-\sqrt{3}$ is outside the given interval. The remaining candidate is $t=\sqrt{3}-1$. Check that its other coordinate derivative is nonzero:

$$
y'(\sqrt{3}-1)=2(\sqrt{3}-1)+2=2\sqrt{3}\ne0.
$$

Therefore, the tangent is vertical at $t=\sqrt{3}-1$.

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\frac{t^2+3}{t-1},\qquad y=t^2+1,\qquad -2<t<4,\quad t\ne1.
$$

Determine all values of $t$ at which the normal to the curve is horizontal. Give exact answers in **ascending order**.

The normal is horizontal at $t=$ {{field-1}} and $t=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The normal is horizontal when the tangent is vertical. We therefore need $x'(t)=0$ and $y'(t)\ne0$ at parameters in the given domain.

Using the quotient rule for $x$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
x'(t)&=\frac{2t(t-1)-(t^2+3)}{(t-1)^2}\\
&=\frac{t^2-2t-3}{(t-1)^2}\\
&=\frac{(t-3)(t+1)}{(t-1)^2},\\
y'(t)&=2t.
\end{aligned}
$$

For $t\ne1$, the denominator of $x'(t)$ is nonzero. Hence $x'(t)=0$ exactly when

$$
(t-3)(t+1)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t=-1\ \text{or}\ t=3.
$$

Both values lie in $-2<t<4$ and neither equals the excluded parameter $1$. The value $t=1$ is not a candidate: the original curve is undefined there.

Check the other derivative:

$$
y'(-1)=-2\ne0,\qquad y'(3)=6\ne0.
$$

Thus the normal is horizontal at $t=-1$ and $t=3$, in that order. Although $y'(0)=0$, we have $x'(0)=-3\ne0$, so $t=0$ gives a horizontal tangent and a vertical normal instead.

x=t^2-6t,\qquad y=t^3+t,\qquad -\infty<t<\infty.
$$

Determine the value of the parameter $t$ at which the normal to the curve is horizontal.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The normal is horizontal when the tangent is vertical. We therefore need $x'(t)=0$ and $y'(t)\ne0$.

Differentiate both coordinates:

$$
x'(t)=2t-6,\qquad y'(t)=3t^2+1.
$$

Solving $x'(t)=0$ gives

$$
2t-6=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t=3.
$$

At this parameter,

$$
y'(3)=3(3)^2+1=28\ne0.
$$

Thus the tangent is vertical and the normal is horizontal at $t=3$.

question.:question/problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
\begin{aligned}
x&=3\cos\left(t-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+2,\\
y&=2\sin\left(t-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)-1,\\
&\hspace{1em}0\le t<2\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

Determine all values of $t$ at which the normal to the curve is vertical. Give exact answers in **ascending order**.

The normal is vertical at $t=$ {{field-1}} and $t=$ {{field-2}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
The normal is vertical when the tangent is horizontal. We therefore need $y'(t)=0$ and $x'(t)\ne0$.

Differentiate both coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x'(t)&=-3\sin\left(t-\frac{\pi}{6}\right),\\
y'(t)&=2\cos\left(t-\frac{\pi}{6}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Set $y'(t)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos\left(t-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)&=0,\\
t-\frac{\pi}{6}&=\frac{\pi}{2}+k\pi,\\
t&=\frac{2\pi}{3}+k\pi,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.
\end{aligned}
$$

Only $k=0$ and $k=1$ place $t$ in $0\le t<2\pi$, giving $t=\frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $t=\frac{5\pi}{3}$. Check the other derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x'\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)&=-3\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=-3\ne0,\\
x'\left(\frac{5\pi}{3}\right)&=-3\sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)=3\ne0.
\end{aligned}
$$

The normal is vertical at $t=\frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $t=\frac{5\pi}{3}$, in that order.
